I have sat in the choir loft of First Baptist Tuscaloosa for 38 years and the Sunday after Easter is the first time I ever watched my husband sit in the back row.

He didn't tell me he was going to do it.

I was tying my robe at the back of the sanctuary when I looked out and saw the top of his head exactly where it shouldn't have been. Last pew. Aisle seat. The seat where the older men who can't sit through a whole service without getting up sit.

Owen has sat in the third pew from the front for 41 years.

Third pew, left side, on the aisle, so he can stand up at the offering plate without making anyone shuffle their knees. That's his pew. The Crenshaw kids know it. The ushers know it. Pastor Ed used to make a joke about it from the pulpit when he first started, said if he ever didn't see Owen Mahoney in that third pew he'd assume the rapture had come and he'd been left behind.

That Sunday I watched him sit in the back row with his hands on his knees and his shoulders rolled forward like he was bracing for something.

And I knew.

I knew he couldn't kneel anymore.

I knew he didn't want anyone to see.

I sang the whole service that morning and I couldn't tell you a single word of a single hymn. I just kept looking at the back of my husband's head and feeling something in my chest collapse in slow motion.

My name is Loretta. I'm 63. I've been married to Owen for 41 years and we live in a yellow brick ranch on a cul de sac off Hargrove Road in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, two miles from the church we got married in. Owen is 64. He's been a deacon at First Baptist since he was 31. He helped pour the foundation of the fellowship hall in 1996. He's served on every committee that exists and a few they invented just because he kept showing up.

He is the most reliable man I have ever known.

When something needs doing at that church, Owen does it. He doesn't wait to be asked. He doesn't make a fuss about it. He just shows up early and stays late and goes home and doesn't tell anyone what he did.

The kneeling thing started in the spring of last year.

It was small at first. He'd come up from the kneeler at the end of communion and grip the back of the pew in front of him like he was steadying himself in a boat. He'd do that thing men do where they pretend it's nothing. Roll the shoulders. Stretch the neck. Crack the knuckles. Like he just chose to grip the pew.

I noticed. He noticed I noticed. Neither of us said anything.

By August it was bad enough that he'd started skipping the kneeling altogether. He'd bend forward and put his elbows on the back of the pew in front and bow his head and pretend he was praying that way on purpose. I'd watch him out of the corner of my eye and I'd know what was happening, but I wouldn't say a word, because Owen Mahoney is a proud man and I have been married long enough to know that telling a proud man you've noticed his pride is hurting is the fastest way to lose him.

By Christmas he was getting up out of his recliner the same way.

Both hands on the armrests. A long breath. A push. A pause halfway up to let the knees catch up.

I'd hear him in the morning before I came out of the bedroom. The chair creaking. The little grunt. The pause. Then his footsteps going slow to the kitchen.

He turned 64 in February. We didn't do anything big. He said he didn't want a fuss. I made his mama's pound cake and we sat at the kitchen table and he told me his knees felt like there was sand in them.

That's the word he used. Sand.

Said it felt like every joint in his body was full of fine grit that ground when he moved.

I asked if he'd talked to Dr. Henley about it.

He said he had.

He said Dr. Henley had told him that at 64 you start to feel things you didn't feel at 50, and that as long as he was managing it with Tylenol and staying active, there wasn't much else to do.

He said Dr. Henley had used the word "wear and tear."

I have come to hate that phrase.

Wear and tear. Like Owen is a tire on the side of the road. Like the man I married, the man who built the back deck on this house with his own two hands, the man who carried my mama up two flights of stairs the night she fell, the man who has knelt in that third pew every Sunday for 41 years asking God to bless our daughters and our grandbabies and the strangers in the back row, is just a worn out part on a machine that's run too many miles.

That's not aging. That's surrender. And the doctor was handing it to him in a paper cup.

After his birthday he started doing something that broke my heart in a quiet, daily way.

He stopped going out to the workshop.

Owen built a workshop in our backyard in 1998. It's a 12 by 16 shed with a peg board wall and a workbench his daddy built him as a wedding gift. He's been out there every Saturday morning of our marriage building cradles for the grandbabies, fixing chairs for ladies in the church, sharpening blades, oiling hinges.

After his birthday he just stopped.

He'd walk past the window in the kitchen, look out at the shed, and keep walking.

I asked him about it one Saturday in March.

He was sitting in his recliner with the morning paper on his lap and he wasn't reading it. He was just holding it.

I sat on the arm of the chair and I said, "Honey, you haven't been out to the shop in a month."

He folded the paper very neatly in half and set it on the side table.

"I can't get down on the floor anymore, Lor. I dropped a chisel last week and I stood there for ten minutes trying to figure out how I was going to pick it up. I had to use the broom to slide it over to the workbench so I could grab it without bending down."

He looked at me. His eyes were tired in a way I hadn't seen before.

"A man who can't pick up his own chisel doesn't belong in a workshop."

I sat on the arm of that chair and I held his hand and I didn't say anything because there wasn't anything to say. The chair creaked when he shifted his weight. I could hear the clock on the mantle. I could hear our beagle Buster snoring on the rug.

I thought about the wedding bench he built for our oldest daughter Maribeth when she got married in 2007. Hand carved. Took him eight months. Sits at the foot of her bed in Birmingham.

I thought about the chair he built for our granddaughter Pearl when she was three and decided she needed a chair "just her size." She's 11 now and the chair sits in the corner of her room with a stuffed elephant on it.

I thought about how, in 41 years, that man has never once not been able to pick something up off the floor.

And the Sunday after Easter he sat in the back row of the church.

That's where things stood when Tabitha invited me to coffee.

Tabitha is the new associate pastor's wife. They moved down to Tuscaloosa from Birmingham in January when Pastor Ed brought her husband Wesley on as a second pastor to help with the youth ministry and the visitation. She's 41, has three kids under ten, and the kind of energy I had when I was 41 and have absolutely forgotten how to access.

She also notices things.

I think that's what struck me about her from the first time I met her in the church kitchen. She watches people. Not in a judgmental way. In a way that makes you feel seen. She'd noticed me, I guess, because the Tuesday after Easter she sent me a text and asked if I'd meet her at the Heritage House café off University Boulevard. Just to talk.

I almost said no.

I'm glad I didn't.

We sat in a booth by the window. She ordered a chai. I ordered a coffee. She let me settle in for about five minutes of small talk before she put her cup down and looked at me and said:

"Loretta, I watched Owen on Sunday. Is he okay?"

I felt my eyes fill up before I could even answer.

She didn't rush me. She just slid a paper napkin across the table and waited.

I told her everything. The kneeling. The back pew. The workshop. The chisel on the floor. The way he'd started getting out of his chair like an old man instead of like Owen. The doctor and his wear and tear. The sand in his joints. The way he'd stopped picking up his grandbabies when they came over and was leaving that to me now, which felt like such a small thing and was the biggest thing.

She listened. The whole time.

When I ran out of words she sat back in the booth and folded her hands around her chai and looked out the window for a minute.

Then she said, "My daddy went through the same thing four years ago."

She told me her daddy was a finish carpenter in Hoover. Worked his whole life with his hands. Started having the same problem with his knees in his early 60s. Same conversation with the same kind of doctor. Same wear and tear. Same Tylenol. Same slow shutting down.

"He was about to retire early because he couldn't get up the ladder anymore," she said. "And then my sister Janelle, who's a hospital pharmacist in Mountain Brook, came home one weekend with something she'd been reading about. She'd been reading about how joints actually work. Like, at the cellular level. The thing my daddy's doctor never once explained to him."

I sat there with my coffee getting cold and I listened.

"She told my daddy that the cells in his joints needed energy to do their job. They need energy to maintain cartilage, to manage inflammation, to stay lubricated. And the place cells get energy from is something called mitochondria, which she said were like little power plants inside every single cell in your body."

I'd heard the word mitochondria before. From a high school biology class 47 years ago. That was about as far as it went for me.

"She said as we get older, and with all the processed food and stress and chemicals we live with now, those little power plants in our cells start to wear down. They don't make energy the way they used to. And the cells in our joints, which need a lot of energy to keep up with all the maintenance they do, are some of the first cells to feel it."

She leaned forward.

"She said it was like trying to deliver lumber to a construction site that didn't have any power. The lumber is sitting in the driveway. The crew is standing around. But nothing is getting built, because there's no power to run the saws."

I just stared at her.

Because I understood that. I understood that in a way I had never understood a single thing a doctor had ever told Owen.

His joints weren't worn out. The cells inside them weren't getting enough power to do their job.

"All the things my daddy had tried," she said, "the glucosamine, the fish oil, the turmeric capsules, the cream you rub on, the cortisone shot, none of it touched the power plant. They were all trying to fix the lumber. Or move the lumber around. Or grease the lumber. They weren't doing anything about the power."

She took a sip of her chai.

"Janelle told him about something called amla. Indian gooseberry. She'd been reading about it in pharmacy research forums she belongs to. She said in the research, amla helps support a pathway in your body called AMPK, which is one of the main switches your body uses to keep those little power plants running properly."

She said when AMPK gets activated, the mitochondria can start making energy more efficiently again. The way they used to. And when energy starts flowing back into the cells in your joints, those cells can finally get back to work, doing what they're designed to do. Maintaining the cartilage. Managing the inflammation. Supporting mobility.

"She told him amla also has one of the highest antioxidant profiles of anything that's ever been measured in a food. So while it's helping the power plants run again, it's also protecting them from the oxidative stress that wore them down in the first place."

She smiled.

"In the old Ayurvedic tradition, they call amla 'the nurse.' Because it doesn't push the body to do anything. It just supports what the body is already designed to do."

I sat in that booth and I felt something I hadn't felt in a year and a half.

I felt hope.

Not the kind of hope where you talk yourself into believing something might work. The kind of hope where, for the first time, somebody has explained the problem in a way that makes sense, and the solution they're describing actually matches the problem.

Owen's joints weren't broken. They were starved.

Tabitha pulled out her phone and showed me the bottle her daddy had been taking for three years now. It was a brand called Auniva. The bottle was dark green. The label said Amla Superfruit Extract.

"He gets it from their website," she said. "Two capsules a day with water. He's been on it since the spring of 2022. He retired last year, but he retired because he wanted to, not because his body forced him to. He's out in his shop right now building a rocking chair for my newest baby. He's 67."

She wrote the website on the back of a napkin and slid it across the table.

auniva.co/amla/33

I sat with that napkin in my purse for two days before I ordered. I don't know why. Maybe because I'd watched my husband try so many things and not one of them had moved the needle and I didn't think I could stand to watch one more bottle line up next to all the other ones on the shelf above the kitchen sink.

But that Thursday, after dinner, I sat on the edge of our bed with my phone and I ordered a bottle.

It came on a Tuesday. A 30 day supply. Two capsules per serving.

I didn't tell Owen what it was when I gave it to him. I told him a friend from church had given it to me and said it was good for energy and the joints and that it was just a berry from India. I told him he didn't have to take it if he didn't want to. He took it because he loves me and because I'd already opened the bottle.

The first week, nothing.

I'll be honest with you. I was watching him like a hawk and I didn't see anything. He went to work. He came home. He sat in his chair. He read the paper. The chair creaked when he got up.

The second week, something small.

It was a Wednesday morning. I came out of the bedroom and Owen was already in the kitchen pouring his coffee. That's not unusual. What was unusual was that he was standing flat footed at the counter, both feet planted, not leaning on anything.

For the last year, when he made his morning coffee, he had been leaning his left hip into the edge of the counter to take the weight off his right knee. Every morning. Without thinking about it. So consistent that there was a faint shiny spot on the trim where his belt buckle had worn the paint.

That Wednesday he was standing up straight.

I didn't say anything. I just got my own cup and kissed his cheek and went and sat at the table.

Week three I caught him in the backyard.

He'd gone out to take Buster to do his business and 20 minutes had passed and he hadn't come back in. I went to the kitchen window to look.

He was standing in the open doorway of the workshop. The doorway he hadn't crossed since March.

He had his hands on his hips and he was looking at the workbench like he was trying to remember how to be the man who used to stand there.

I didn't go out. I let him have that moment alone. I went back to the kitchen and I cried at the sink.

He came back in 30 minutes later and didn't say anything about it. But that Saturday I heard the workshop door open and close, and I heard a saw running, and at lunchtime he came in with sawdust on his forearms and a small wooden box in his hands. About the size of a recipe card box. Pine. Hand cut dovetails. Not finished yet. Just the box.

He set it on the kitchen table.

"For Pearl," he said. "She's been wanting one for her hair ribbons."

He sat down at the table and ate a sandwich and he didn't make a big deal out of it.

I made a big deal out of it inside.

By week five he was kneeling again.

Sunday morning. Communion. I was up in the choir loft and I watched him come down out of the pew, the third pew from the front, his pew, and lower himself onto the kneeler and bow his head over his folded hands.

He came up on his own. No hand on the back of the pew in front.

He just stood up.

The way Owen Mahoney stands up.

I sang "Be Thou My Vision" with tears running down my face and the lady next to me, Mrs. Patterson, leaned over and asked if I was alright and I just nodded because there were no words.

By the end of the second month he was out in the workshop every Saturday again. He built Pearl's hair ribbon box. He built a step stool for our youngest granddaughter Hattie. He started on a porch swing he says he wants to give to our daughter Maribeth for her birthday in November.

He picked up Hattie at Easter dinner this year. Carried her on his hip into the dining room. She's three and a half and she's been ours to spoil since the day she was born, and I had not seen Owen carry that child in over a year. He sat her on his knee at the table and fed her cornbread out of his hand.

His knees don't have sand in them anymore.

He didn't say that. He doesn't talk about it directly, the way men of his generation don't talk about things directly. But the other night he was getting up out of his recliner and he just stood up, no hands on the armrests, no pause, no grunt, and he caught my eye and gave me a little half smile and said, "Well, look at that."

That was as close as he'll ever come to telling me.

I have not had to lift a grandbaby up to him in months.

I want to tell you something, and I want to tell you carefully, because I know how the world is.

I'm not telling you Auniva's Amla is a miracle. I'm not telling you it's a cure for anything. I'm telling you that my husband has been on it for almost five months now, and the man I had been quietly grieving is back in his pew, back in his workshop, back on the floor with his grandbabies.

I'm telling you that for the first time in two years, somebody explained to me why his joints were giving out in a way that actually made sense. That his cells were running out of power. That the maintenance crew was still inside him, still ready to work, but the lights were off and the saws weren't running. And that there's something that can help turn the lights back on, gently, the way the body is already designed to.

I'm telling you that amla is "the nurse" and that's exactly what it has felt like in our house. Quiet. Steady. Showing up every day. Not pushing. Just supporting.

If your husband is doing the chair grunt. If he's leaning on the counter when he pours his coffee. If he's stopped going out to the shop, or the garage, or the boat, or the yard. If he's started sitting in the back row.

If your doctor has told you it's wear and tear and to take a Tylenol and move along.

I'd ask you to do what I did, which is sit with it for two days and then order one bottle.

auniva.co/amla/33

It's a 30 day supply. Two capsules a day with water. It's a small company and they have a 90 day money back guarantee, which I didn't even know about until I went to reorder and saw it on their site. If it doesn't do anything for him in three months, you return it and they refund you. That's it. No questions. No subscription you have to call and cancel. Just send it back.

I have ordered Owen's third bottle. I keep a spare on the shelf above the kitchen sink, right next to all the bottles that didn't work, like a little trophy.

He pulled into our driveway in a white pickup truck with a porch swing in the bed that he had built for Tabitha as a housewarming gift. He's 67. He carried that swing into the backyard by himself. Owen helped him hang it. The two of them stood there afterward looking at it, two old finish carpenters with sawdust on their forearms, and I watched them from the kitchen window and I thought about how close we'd come to never having that afternoon.

A company that will give you 90 days to decide if something is working for your husband is a company that believes in what's in the bottle. That's not how the system works. That's how Auniva works.

My mother died at home over 11 days. I took the night shift because nobody else would. On night 8, at 4 in the morning, I caught the mistake.

There is a kitchen chair in my garage that I have not been able to throw away.

It's the one I put beside her bed. My husband has asked twice whether it's going, and twice I've said not yet.

My name is Carol. I'm 62.

My mother died in March, at home, in what used to be the dining room.

I'm not going to make this beautiful. It wasn't.

Anybody who's done it knows it wasn't.

What I want to talk about is the nights, because that's the part nobody prepares you for and the part I got asked to do.

There were 4 of us. My brother, his wife, my sister, me.

You split it up. Somebody does mornings, somebody does the afternoon, somebody handles the phone calls and the forms.

And then there's the night, and everybody looks at the floor.

I said I'd do the nights. Not because I'm brave.

Because I was the only one who wasn't working.

Here's what I need to establish, because otherwise the rest of this sounds like I'm bragging.

I have never been good at being awake.

I'm the person who can't watch a film past 9. I fell asleep at my own 40th.

My family has an actual running joke about it.

So the idea of me doing 11 nights in a row - 10pm to 7am, alone, responsible - was, frankly, a poor plan.

Back up 5 months.

I'd been on a mushroom coffee since the October before. My daughter put me on it.

The reason was boring. I'd stopped being able to do anything after 2 in the afternoon, and I'd been waking at 3 in the morning with my heart going for no reason I could name.

Went to the doctor twice. Blood's fine.

Told it was normal for my age and sent home.

So I'd decided I was just a woman who'd gone soft, and I stopped mentioning it.

By March I'd honestly half-forgotten I was drinking it.

The afternoons had quietly stopped being a problem and I'd stopped noticing there had ever been one.

Then my mother started dying, and I found out what it had been doing.

I'll tell you what a hospice night actually is.

It is not dramatic. That's the thing.

It's a chair, a lamp turned away from the bed, and a very long stretch of time.

You listen to breathing. That's the whole job.

You listen to breathing and you do not fall asleep.

You turn her every couple of hours. You do the mouth swabs.

You write down the time of everything on a sheet the nurse leaves.

And between those things there is nothing at all, for 40 minutes at a stretch, in a dark room, at 3 in the morning, when every part of your body is telling you to stop.

I drank a cup of that mushroom coffee at 9pm before every single one of those nights.

I'm aware that is not what it's for. I'm aware you're supposed to have it in the morning.

I didn't care. It was the only thing I had that worked.

Night 8.

The visiting nurse had been in that afternoon and there'd been a changeover - a different nurse from the one we'd had all week.

She left the handover sheet on the side like they do, with the times written on it.

At about 4 in the morning I was copying her last dose onto my sheet and something didn't sit right.

The interval on the handover sheet and the interval on the pharmacy label were not the same.

Now. I want to be careful here, because I'm not a nurse and this is not me being clever.

It was a 10-second thing. Two numbers next to each other that didn't match.

But you have to be awake to see two numbers not matching at 4 in the morning, and I was.

I called the after-hours line. They checked it.

The handover sheet was wrong.

They were very kind about it and told me it happens, and that I'd done the right thing calling.

I sat back down in that chair and shook for about 20 minutes.

She died on the 11th night, about 5:30 in the morning, and I was awake for it.

That matters to me more than I can explain to you.

She wasn't alone and she wasn't with somebody asleep in a chair. She was with her daughter, who was awake.

Afterwards I fell apart properly for about 3 weeks.

Flat, weepy, sleeping 11 hours and waking up tired, couldn't hold a thought.

Which I now understand is just what happens when you've been running on stress hormones for two weeks and then it stops.

But during it, I was a person I have never been.

So when it was over I sat down and worked out what was actually different about me.

And the only thing I could find was a cup of something I'd been drinking since October.

Then I read about it for a month, because I wanted to know whether I'd imagined it.

Cortisol is the stress hormone. It's supposed to move.

High in the morning to get you up. Sloping down across the day.

Lowest in the middle of the night.

That slope is what being a functioning person actually is.

Past 50, your body clears it more slowly. So instead of a slope you get a plateau.

It goes up in the morning and then it just stays up.

Flat at 2 in the afternoon, because there's no peak left to spend.

I HATE taking showers.

ok I need to talk about this because I feel like no one says it out loud. I would literally sit on my bed for an hour knowing I needed to shower and just… not do it. and it's not like I didn't know I was gross. I KNEW. but my brain would start listing every single step like ok you gotta get up, take your clothes off, get cold, wait for the water, wash your hair which means you gotta dry it later, and by step 4 I'm already exhausted and I haven't even stood up yet. I genuinely thought I was just a lazy disgusting person until I got diagnosed and found out this is literally an executive function thing. like my brain treats showering as 15 separate tasks instead of one. anyway I saw someone on tiktok showering with the lights off with some little glowy lamp and I was like ok that's weird but also I haven't showered in 3 days so let me just try it. I got this little mushroom lamp and put it on my shower shelf and turned everything off. I swear to god something shifted. like my whole body just relaxed in a way it never does in the shower. no buzzy overhead light, no bright white everything, just warm steam and this soft glow and suddenly I'm standing there actually enjoying it?? I literally have to drag myself OUT now. that's the plot twist no one warned me about.

My mother died at home over 11 days. I took the night shift because nobody else would. On night 8, at 4 in the morning, I caught the mistake.

There is a kitchen chair in my garage that I have not been able to throw away.

It's the one I put beside her bed. My husband has asked twice whether it's going, and twice I've said not yet.

My name is Carol. I'm 62.

My mother died in March, at home, in what used to be the dining room.

I'm not going to make this beautiful. It wasn't.

Anybody who's done it knows it wasn't.

What I want to talk about is the nights, because that's the part nobody prepares you for and the part I got asked to do.

There were 4 of us. My brother, his wife, my sister, me.

You split it up. Somebody does mornings, somebody does the afternoon, somebody handles the phone calls and the forms.

And then there's the night, and everybody looks at the floor.

I said I'd do the nights. Not because I'm brave.

Because I was the only one who wasn't working.

Here's what I need to establish, because otherwise the rest of this sounds like I'm bragging.

I have never been good at being awake.

I'm the person who can't watch a film past 9. I fell asleep at my own 40th.

My family has an actual running joke about it.

So the idea of me doing 11 nights in a row - 10pm to 7am, alone, responsible - was, frankly, a poor plan.

Back up 5 months.

I'd been on a mushroom coffee since the October before. My daughter put me on it.

It is not dramatic. That's the thing.

It's a chair, a lamp turned away from the bed, and a very long stretch of time.

The interval on the handover sheet and the interval on the pharmacy label were not the same.

It was a 10-second thing. Two numbers next to each other that didn't match.

But you have to be awake to see two numbers not matching at 4 in the morning, and I was.

I called the after-hours line. They checked it.

The handover sheet was wrong.

They were very kind about it and told me it happens, and that I'd done the right thing calling.

I sat back down in that chair and shook for about 20 minutes.

She died on the 11th night, about 5:30 in the morning, and I was awake for it.

That matters to me more than I can explain to you.

She wasn't alone and she wasn't with somebody asleep in a chair. She was with her daughter, who was awake.

Afterwards I fell apart properly for about 3 weeks.

Flat, weepy, sleeping 11 hours and waking up tired, couldn't hold a thought.

Which I now understand is just what happens when you've been running on stress hormones for two weeks and then it stops.

High in the morning to get you up. Sloping down across the day.

Lowest in the middle of the night.

That slope is what being a functioning person actually is.

It goes up in the morning and then it just stays up.

bodyText:
I thought my urologist was messing with me when he finally pulled up this diagram.

At 51, I had convinced myself my body just did not work anymore.

You know that thing where you turn out the bedside lamp before your wife walks into the bedroom?

You do it because you do not want her to see you standing there hopeful.

And then you do not want her to watch what happens next, or what does not happen.

You know that feeling when you catch your own reflection in a dark car window at a red light on the way home from work?

Something deep inside your chest tightens.

You realize your father looked exactly that tired and defeated at the exact same age.

Or when your wife reaches for you in the middle of the night the way she used to.

Your very first reflex is to lie completely still and pretend you are already in a deep sleep.

You do that so she does not feel what failed to happen under the sheets.

That was my daily reality.

For four agonizing years.

And here is the exact thing that made the whole nightmare ten times worse.

I was doing every single thing right.

I am not a guy who let himself go or ignored his health.

I was the exact opposite.

I ate completely clean five days a week.

I kept my LDL cholesterol under 130 using a strict Mediterranean diet without cheating.

I lifted weights three days a week at the local gym.

I ran two days a week on the treadmill.

I made sure I got a minimum of seven hours of sleep every single night.

I cut out beer entirely.

I even started doing guided meditation in the mornings to control my cortisol levels.

I went to my annual physical every single year like clockwork.

My primary care doctor smiled, patted me on the back, and told me I was in the top ten percent for my age bracket.

It did not matter at all.

The physical response down below just kept fading.

Slowly.

Quietly.

One quarter at a time.

I tried the standard 50mg prescription my urologist wrote when I first brought it up at age 48.

It worked for about eight months.

Then it started losing its punch and needing a bump.

My doctor doubled the prescription to 100mg.

That worked for another ten or twelve months.

Then it started becoming completely inconsistent.

Some nights it worked halfway.

Other nights it gave me a pounding headache, flushed red cheeks, a stuffed-up nose, and zero physical response below the belt.

I tried L-arginine powders that tasted like chalk.

I drank sour beetroot powder mixed into cold water every morning.

I bought an eighty-nine dollar nitric oxide booster from a health brand I heard on a popular podcast.

I tried a low-dose testosterone protocol that my urologist admitted I did not clinically need based on my lab work, but suggested I test anyway.

I spent twenty-eight hundred dollars on a six-week executive wellness retreat that included freezing cold plunges, infrared saunas, and something they called vascular optimization coaching.

I calculated the receipts last winter.

I spent over forty-six hundred dollars over four years on things that either did nothing, or worked for two weeks before my body slid right back to where it started.

And through all of that wasted money and private shame, I kept asking myself the exact same question.

If my diet is clean, and my testosterone is normal, and my body weight is healthy, what on earth is actually wrong with me?

Because I was working harder on my physical body at 51 than I ever worked at 31.

And my body was flatly refusing to answer.

My wife never criticized me.

She never said a hurtful word.

She was gentle and kind, which somehow made the humiliation hurt even more.

I started pulling away from her without even realizing I was doing it.

I stayed downstairs reading on my tablet until she was already fast asleep upstairs.

I started getting dressed in the morning with the bathroom door firmly closed.

I began turning slightly away whenever she walked up and tried to hug me while I was making coffee in the kitchen.

I made up an excuse to say no to the weekend cabin trip her sister invited us on.

I made an awkward joke to change the subject when my younger brother talked about a romantic beach getaway he was planning with his wife.

We slowly transitioned from a couple who could barely keep our hands off each other into two roommates.

Two polite people who kissed each other dryly on the cheek in the morning and watched different shows on our phones from opposite ends of the couch at night.

She convinced herself that something was wrong with our marriage.

She thought I was no longer attracted to her.

She thought I was pulling away because she had gotten older.

I knew the agonizing truth.

Nothing was wrong with our love, but my physical machinery was broken.

Finally, I could not take the silence anymore.

I went back to my urologist and demanded that he run every comprehensive blood panel available.

Full lipid breakdown.

Total testosterone.

Free testosterone.

PSA levels for my prostate.

Fasting blood glucose.

Hemoglobin A1c.

High-sensitivity inflammation markers.

Every test in the book that you order for a 51-year-old man.

I sat in his office and told him I had been living through this nightmare for four years and I needed a real medical explanation.

Two weeks later, the results arrived.

Every single marker came back in the normal green range.

My doctor looked across his desk, shrugged his shoulders, and leaned back in his chair.

He told me that erectile reliability naturally drops off after fifty.

He told me to stop stressing over it and just keep taking the 100mg blue pill whenever we wanted to be intimate.

That was the entire eight-minute consultation.

I walked out of the medical building, sat in my truck in the parking lot, and gripped the steering wheel with both hands for fifteen minutes.

I felt completely abandoned by the medical system.

I knew that if I just kept doing what he said, in another three years I would be completely numb.

That evening, I called my brother.

He had gone through a serious circulation scare two years earlier and told me to see a specialist who looked at the human body through fluid mechanics rather than quick drug scripts.

He gave me the name of Dr. Sullivan, a board-certified vascular medicine specialist who had spent thirty years studying arterial flow and micro-vascular resistance.

I called his clinic the next morning.

I told his scheduling nurse that I was not leaving his office until a doctor looked me in the eye and explained the physical mechanics of why my body was failing.

When my appointment day arrived, Dr. Sullivan sat down and listened to my entire story without glancing at his watch once.

He looked over my four years of normal lab work.

He listened to the list of supplements, the diet, the workouts, and the escalating prescription doses.

When I finally finished speaking, he was quiet for a few moments.

Then he swiveled his large desktop monitor directly toward me.

I am going to show you something, he said.

Because what you are dealing with is something that ninety-five percent of men your age are never told about until they are sitting in an exam room being handed an injection needle or an implant brochure.

On the screen was an anatomical cross-section diagram of a human blood vessel.

It showed a cross-cut view of a single micro-artery.

Around the inside perimeter was a paper-thin layer of cells.

And coating the interior wall of that vessel was a thick, jagged, yellowish-gray sludge that narrowed the opening down to a tiny pinhole.

Small red arrows showed blood trying to squeeze through the restriction, backing up and slowing to a sluggish crawl.

Your erectile tissue is not the problem, Dr. Sullivan told me flatly.

The pipes feeding that tissue are the problem.

He pointed his pen directly at the inner cellular lining on the diagram.

Those microscopic pipes are lined with a delicate single layer of specialized cells called the vascular endothelium.

When you are young and your vessels are clean, that endothelial layer produces a signaling molecule called nitric oxide.

Nitric oxide is the chemical trigger that commands the smooth muscle walls of the artery to relax and expand wide open.

When you were thirty years old, that signal fired on demand within seconds and your circulatory system delivered full hydraulic pressure instantly.

Then Dr. Sullivan clicked to the second slide on his screen.

This diagram showed two different arteries side by side.

On the left was a coronary artery feeding the heart, measuring between three and four millimeters across.

On the right was a pudendal micro-artery feeding male pelvic tissue, measuring barely one to two millimeters across.

Look at the difference in pipe diameter, Dr. Sullivan said.

Starting around age forty, arterial plaque and tough cross-linked protein sludge quietly begin accumulating on the interior walls of your circulatory system.

The arteries feeding your pelvic erectile tissue are only one to two millimeters wide.

They are the narrowest functional high-pressure arteries in your entire body.

Think about basic fluid plumbing for a moment.

The exact same layer of plaque that would take twenty-five years to cause a noticeable restriction in a four-millimeter coronary artery will choke a one-millimeter pelvic artery in just a few years.

Long before a man feels tightness in his chest or fails a treadmill stress test, his one-millimeter micro-arteries are already seventy percent restricted.

And once that delicate endothelial lining is coated with inflammatory sludge, it can no longer manufacture nitric oxide.

The pipe is anatomically still present in your body.

It simply cannot expand when called upon.

I sat there staring at the screen as the truth hit me like a physical punch.

I asked him why none of my previous blood tests had ever shown this buildup.

Dr. Sullivan shook his head and gave a tired smile.

Because standard urology and primary care blood panels do not measure the physical interior of your micro-arteries, he answered.

A total testosterone test measures hormone levels circulating in your serum, not arterial lumen diameter.

A PSA test measures prostate protein leakage, not micro-vascular wall inflammation.

A standard fasting lipid panel measures cholesterol floating in your blood, not the hardened cross-linked plaque that has already cemented itself against your vessel walls.

That is why your doctor looked at your normal labs and shrugged.

You do not have a testosterone deficiency.

You do not have a mental block or performance anxiety.

You have vasculogenic erectile decline.

It is a mechanical plumbing failure caused by physical sludge coating the smallest arteries in your body.

And not a single pharmaceutical pill or testosterone injection on earth clears that sludge out of the pipe.

I sat in that chair and let those words sink deep into my chest.

Four years of self-doubt.

Four years of wondering if I was losing my manhood.

Four years of quietly hating my own body and feeling like an inadequate husband.

It was never a lack of willpower.

It was never a lack of desire for my wife.

It was a physical blockage in a one-millimeter pipe.

And then Dr. Sullivan broke down why every single thing I had tried over those four years had inevitably failed.

Consider what the blue pill actually does, he said.

Viagra and Cialis work by inhibiting an enzyme called PDE5, which temporarily prevents the breakdown of whatever nitric oxide signal is already present.

It is an amplifier, not a generator.

The pill cannot force your endothelial lining to produce new nitric oxide if the cells are suffocating under a blanket of plaque.

So when you first start taking it, the drug amplifies the thirty percent signal you have left and you get a temporary result.

But as the years pass and the sludge continues to accumulate, your underlying nitric oxide output drops from thirty percent to twenty percent, then to ten percent.

Eventually, the drug has almost nothing left to amplify.

That is why you had to double your dose to 100mg.

And that is why the 100mg dose was starting to fail.

Then he explained testosterone replacement.

Taking testosterone when your micro-arteries are choked with plaque is like turning up the main city water valve on the street when the pipe running into your house is choked with mineral scale.

You can crank the pressure to the absolute maximum.

You might get a brief burst of rusty water for three seconds.

Then the flow slows right back down to a hopeless trickle because the physical bottleneck is inside the pipe.

High testosterone cannot push blood through a blocked one-millimeter straw.

He walked through the rest of the list.

L-arginine and beetroot provide dietary precursors, but if the endothelial enzyme is blocked by cellular inflammation, your body cannot convert those precursors into blood flow.

Statins may slow down the accumulation of fresh soft cholesterol, but peer-reviewed clinical data shows they do almost nothing to dissolve old, hardened, fibrous plaque that has been sitting there for a decade.

And cold plunges, saunas, and wellness retreats might make you feel invigorated for an hour, but they cannot physically dissolve arterial cement.

If a man does not clear the physical sludge out of those one-millimeter vessels, the disease process marches steadily forward.

First the morning response disappears.

Then intimacy requires maximum pharmaceutical stimulation.

Then the pills stop working altogether.

Then the urologist brings up intracavernous needle injections or surgical penile implants.

And within three to five years after pelvic micro-arteries choke off, the exact same vascular restriction begins showing up in the larger coronary arteries feeding the heart.

Erectile decline is the body's earliest vascular warning light.

I looked at Dr. Sullivan and asked the only question that mattered.

How do you physically clear the pipe?

He clicked his mouse and brought up a published clinical research paper on his monitor.

You have to understand what arterial plaque is actually made of, he explained.

Most people believe plaque is just soft butter-like fat sticking to a wall.

That is completely wrong.

Arterial plaque is held together by an extremely tough, web-like mesh of an insoluble protein called fibrin.

Fibrin is the exact same cross-linked protein your body uses to form tough fibrous scabs when you cut your skin.

When your micro-arteries experience microscopic inflammation from aging, blood pressure friction, and daily metabolic stress, your body sends fibrin to patch the area.

The problem is that circulating calcium, cellular debris, and oxidized lipids get trapped inside that fibrous spiderweb.

Over months and years, that mixture hardens into a dense, cement-like sludge that lines the arterial wall.

The human body possesses only one single natural enzyme capable of breaking down cross-linked fibrin.

That enzyme is called plasmin.

When you are twenty-five years old, your vascular system produces abundant plasmin, which immediately sweeps away excess fibrin before it can accumulate into plaque.

But by age fifty, your body's natural plasmin production has plummeted by over sixty percent.

At the exact same time, a blocking protein called PAI-1 increases dramatically, effectively shutting down your natural cleanup crew.

Without active plasmin, fibrin accumulates unchecked inside your narrowest vessels.

The only way to reverse this restriction is to introduce an active, proven fibrinolytic enzyme directly into your bloodstream.

An enzyme that seeks out cross-linked fibrin mesh, dissolves the bonds, and allows the arterial wall to open back up.

There is only one natural compound on the planet clinically demonstrated to perform that exact biological task.

It is an enzyme called Nattokinase.

My mother died at home over 11 days. I took the night shift because nobody else would. On night 8, at 4 in the morning, I caught the mistake.

There is a kitchen chair in my garage that I have not been able to throw away.

It's the one I put beside her bed. My husband has asked twice whether it's going, and twice I've said not yet.

My name is Carol. I'm 62.

My mother died in March, at home, in what used to be the dining room.

I'm not going to make this beautiful. It wasn't.

Anybody who's done it knows it wasn't.

What I want to talk about is the nights, because that's the part nobody prepares you for and the part I got asked to do.

There were 4 of us. My brother, his wife, my sister, me.

You split it up. Somebody does mornings, somebody does the afternoon, somebody handles the phone calls and the forms.

And then there's the night, and everybody looks at the floor.

I said I'd do the nights. Not because I'm brave.

Because I was the only one who wasn't working.

Here's what I need to establish, because otherwise the rest of this sounds like I'm bragging.

I have never been good at being awake.

I'm the person who can't watch a film past 9. I fell asleep at my own 40th.

My family has an actual running joke about it.

So the idea of me doing 11 nights in a row - 10pm to 7am, alone, responsible - was, frankly, a poor plan.

Back up 5 months.

I'd been on a mushroom coffee since the October before. My daughter put me on it.

The reason was boring. I'd stopped being able to do anything after 2 in the afternoon, and I'd been waking at 3 in the morning with my heart going for no reason I could name.

Went to the doctor twice. Blood's fine.

Told it was normal for my age and sent home.

So I'd decided I was just a woman who'd gone soft, and I stopped mentioning it.

By March I'd honestly half-forgotten I was drinking it.

The afternoons had quietly stopped being a problem and I'd stopped noticing there had ever been one.

Then my mother started dying, and I found out what it had been doing.

I'll tell you what a hospice night actually is.

It is not dramatic. That's the thing.

It's a chair, a lamp turned away from the bed, and a very long stretch of time.

You listen to breathing. That's the whole job.

You listen to breathing and you do not fall asleep.

You turn her every couple of hours. You do the mouth swabs.

You write down the time of everything on a sheet the nurse leaves.

And between those things there is nothing at all, for 40 minutes at a stretch, in a dark room, at 3 in the morning, when every part of your body is telling you to stop.

I drank a cup of that mushroom coffee at 9pm before every single one of those nights.

I'm aware that is not what it's for. I'm aware you're supposed to have it in the morning.

I didn't care. It was the only thing I had that worked.

Night 8.

The visiting nurse had been in that afternoon and there'd been a changeover - a different nurse from the one we'd had all week.

She left the handover sheet on the side like they do, with the times written on it.

At about 4 in the morning I was copying her last dose onto my sheet and something didn't sit right.

The interval on the handover sheet and the interval on the pharmacy label were not the same.

Now. I want to be careful here, because I'm not a nurse and this is not me being clever.

It was a 10-second thing. Two numbers next to each other that didn't match.

But you have to be awake to see two numbers not matching at 4 in the morning, and I was.

I called the after-hours line. They checked it.

The handover sheet was wrong.

They were very kind about it and told me it happens, and that I'd done the right thing calling.

I sat back down in that chair and shook for about 20 minutes.

She died on the 11th night, about 5:30 in the morning, and I was awake for it.

That matters to me more than I can explain to you.

She wasn't alone and she wasn't with somebody asleep in a chair. She was with her daughter, who was awake.

Afterwards I fell apart properly for about 3 weeks.

Flat, weepy, sleeping 11 hours and waking up tired, couldn't hold a thought.

Which I now understand is just what happens when you've been running on stress hormones for two weeks and then it stops.

But during it, I was a person I have never been.

So when it was over I sat down and worked out what was actually different about me.

And the only thing I could find was a cup of something I'd been drinking since October.

Then I read about it for a month, because I wanted to know whether I'd imagined it.

Cortisol is the stress hormone. It's supposed to move.

High in the morning to get you up. Sloping down across the day.

Lowest in the middle of the night.

That slope is what being a functioning person actually is.

Past 50, your body clears it more slowly. So instead of a slope you get a plateau.

It goes up in the morning and then it just stays up.

Flat at 2 in the afternoon, because there's no peak left to spend.

Awake at 3 in the morning, because there's no trough coming.

That was my whole complaint before any of this started. And it was one thing, not two.

And here is the part that actually explains night 8.

3 in the morning is the bottom of the curve. It is the hour your body is built to be least awake.

If you're already sitting flat at the top of your range all day, you have got nothing left to spend at 4am.

You don't fall asleep, necessarily. You just stop being able to see two numbers that don't match.

I'm not going to tell you a cup of coffee got me through my mother's death. Nothing gets you through that.

What it did was much smaller and much more specific. It kept me the kind of awake where I was still useful.

The thing I'd been drinking since October is Erth Superfood Brew.

It's real coffee, just low-acid.

600mg of KSM-66 ashwagandha, which is the standardized extract the human trials used. That's the one for cortisol.

500mg of lion's mane. Cordyceps, turkey tail, and real collagen.

Properly dosed and 3rd party tested, which is the reason I picked it over the others.

Plenty of bags say 2,000mg of 6 mushrooms and never tell you the split. It could be 1,900 of the cheapest one.

Plenty print the word ashwagandha, which on its own means almost nothing.

The ones naming KSM-66 were mostly nowhere near 600mg. I found 250mg in other brands more than once.

That's less than half the amount that actually makes a difference.

Here's the last thing.

I'd half-forgotten I was drinking it. That's the honest risk with something that works slowly - you stop noticing, and then you stop buying it.

I found out what it had been doing on the 8 nights it mattered.

On a rainy Friday night in November, I stood in my bathroom holding an alcohol swab and a thirty-gauge needle, getting ready to stab myself in the groin so I could make love to my wife.

It clattered against the drain with a cold, metallic ring.

Through the locked door, I could hear Laura turning pages of a magazine in our bedroom.

She only knew that six months earlier, my prescription blue pills had stopped working completely.

"Robert, your vascular inflow has collapsed."

"At fifty-six, oral pills cannot push blood past that kind of resistance anymore."

"You have two options left."

"You can inject this prostaglandin compound directly into the shaft ten minutes before intercourse."

"Or we can schedule you for surgery and install an inflatable penile implant with a manual saline pump inside your scrotum."

He slid a glossy surgical brochure across his mahogany desk.

The brochure showed diagrams of silicone cylinders being surgically inserted into erectile tissue.

It looked like something out of a horror movie.

I stood there in my bathroom staring at that needle in the sink, feeling an overwhelming wave of nausea.

I was fifty-six years old.

I was an aerospace mechanical engineer.

I had spent thirty-one years designing high-pressure hydraulic fluid systems for commercial aircraft.

And here I was, locked in my own bathroom, treating my own body like a broken piece of scrap metal.

I threw the syringe into the bathroom trash can.

I walked out into the bedroom, turned off the lamp, and climbed under the blankets without saying a word.

When Laura reached over and touched my arm, I pretended I was already asleep.

I lay in the dark with my eyes open until 4:00 AM, staring at the ceiling fan.

Thinking about the twenty-nine years Laura and I had built together.

Thinking about how confident and alive I used to feel in my twenties and thirties.

And wondering how my body had decayed into complete silence.

Until that night, I had no idea that my bedroom failure was not an isolated aging problem.

I had no idea that my body had been taking a daily physical measurement for over thirty years.

A daily pressure reading of the narrowest blood vessel in the entire human body.

And when that vessel backed up, my doctor gave me a chemical pump override and ignored the clogged pipe.

What he never told me, and what pharmaceutical companies spent twenty-five years hiding behind multi-billion-dollar marketing campaigns, is that an erection is not a hormone problem.

It is not an emotional issue.

It is not a character flaw.

An erection is pure mechanical hydraulics.

And the exact same insoluble protein sludge that choked my bedroom blood flow is the exact same sludge that blocks the main artery feeding your heart three years later.

This is documented cardiovascular physics.

Before 1998, when Pfizer launched a synthetic chemical compound that turned male blood flow into a lifelong monthly subscription, physicians knew that the narrowest blood vessels always fail first.

And long before that, before John D. Rockefeller funded the 1910 Flexner Report and pushed natural food enzyme medicine out of American universities, doctors used natural proteolytic compounds to dissolve internal arterial webs before they could ever choke off a man's circulation.

Rockefeller realized you cannot patent a natural enzyme found in traditional fermented foods.

Pfizer realized you cannot charge a man fifteen dollars a pill if you actually dissolve the physical sludge inside his vascular system.

So they built a medical model that sells you a four-hour chemical override while allowing the physical sludge inside your arteries to harden into concrete.

Until four months ago, I was trapped inside that exact pipeline.

I started noticing the decline when I was forty-six.

Up until forty-five, mornings were automatic.

I woke up with strong, natural stiffness every single day.

If someone had told me my vascular system was beginning to choke off, I would have laughed in their face.

That is the most dangerous part of this entire biological trap.

At age forty-five, the insoluble web is already weaving itself across the lining of your arteries, but your vessels are still wide enough that you feel zero pain.

By age forty-nine, morning erections were down to three or four days a week.

I blamed the usual excuses that men use to comfort themselves.

I told myself I was working fifty hours a week at the engineering plant.

I was carrying an extra ten pounds.

The physical sensation felt muffled and distant.

"That is the cavernosal artery running through the base of your pelvis."

"The micro-artery that delivers the hydraulic pressure required for male firmness."

"Do you know the diameter of that vessel?"

"It is barely 1.2 millimeters across."

"It is less than one third the width of the artery feeding your chest."

He pointed the pen at the smaller circle.

"To achieve full, natural firmness, your body must push six times its resting blood volume through a channel barely 1.2 millimeters wide."

"And what happens when insoluble protein sludge begins building up inside your circulatory system?"

My mother died at home over 11 days. I took the night shift because nobody else would. On night 8, at 4 in the morning, I caught the mistake.

There is a kitchen chair in my garage that I have not been able to throw away.

It's the one I put beside her bed. My husband has asked twice whether it's going, and twice I've said not yet.

My name is Carol. I'm 62.

My mother died in March, at home, in what used to be the dining room.

I'm not going to make this beautiful. It wasn't.

Anybody who's done it knows it wasn't.

What I want to talk about is the nights, because that's the part nobody prepares you for and the part I got asked to do.

There were 4 of us. My brother, his wife, my sister, me.

You split it up. Somebody does mornings, somebody does the afternoon, somebody handles the phone calls and the forms.

And then there's the night, and everybody looks at the floor.

I said I'd do the nights. Not because I'm brave.

Because I was the only one who wasn't working.

Here's what I need to establish, because otherwise the rest of this sounds like I'm bragging.

I have never been good at being awake.

I'm the person who can't watch a film past 9. I fell asleep at my own 40th.

My family has an actual running joke about it.

So the idea of me doing 11 nights in a row - 10pm to 7am, alone, responsible - was, frankly, a poor plan.

Back up 5 months.

I'd been on a mushroom coffee since the October before. My daughter put me on it.

The reason was boring. I'd stopped being able to do anything after 2 in the afternoon, and I'd been waking at 3 in the morning with my heart going for no reason I could name.

Went to the doctor twice. Blood's fine.

Told it was normal for my age and sent home.

So I'd decided I was just a woman who'd gone soft, and I stopped mentioning it.

By March I'd honestly half-forgotten I was drinking it.

The afternoons had quietly stopped being a problem and I'd stopped noticing there had ever been one.

Then my mother started dying, and I found out what it had been doing.

I'll tell you what a hospice night actually is.

It is not dramatic. That's the thing.

It's a chair, a lamp turned away from the bed, and a very long stretch of time.

You listen to breathing. That's the whole job.

You listen to breathing and you do not fall asleep.

You turn her every couple of hours. You do the mouth swabs.

You write down the time of everything on a sheet the nurse leaves.

And between those things there is nothing at all, for 40 minutes at a stretch, in a dark room, at 3 in the morning, when every part of your body is telling you to stop.

I drank a cup of that mushroom coffee at 9pm before every single one of those nights.

I'm aware that is not what it's for. I'm aware you're supposed to have it in the morning.

I didn't care. It was the only thing I had that worked.

Night 8.

The visiting nurse had been in that afternoon and there'd been a changeover - a different nurse from the one we'd had all week.

She left the handover sheet on the side like they do, with the times written on it.

At about 4 in the morning I was copying her last dose onto my sheet and something didn't sit right.

The interval on the handover sheet and the interval on the pharmacy label were not the same.

Now. I want to be careful here, because I'm not a nurse and this is not me being clever.

It was a 10-second thing. Two numbers next to each other that didn't match.

But you have to be awake to see two numbers not matching at 4 in the morning, and I was.

I called the after-hours line. They checked it.

The handover sheet was wrong.

They were very kind about it and told me it happens, and that I'd done the right thing calling.

I sat back down in that chair and shook for about 20 minutes.

She died on the 11th night, about 5:30 in the morning, and I was awake for it.

That matters to me more than I can explain to you.

She wasn't alone and she wasn't with somebody asleep in a chair. She was with her daughter, who was awake.

Afterwards I fell apart properly for about 3 weeks.

Flat, weepy, sleeping 11 hours and waking up tired, couldn't hold a thought.

Which I now understand is just what happens when you've been running on stress hormones for two weeks and then it stops.

But during it, I was a person I have never been.

So when it was over I sat down and worked out what was actually different about me.

And the only thing I could find was a cup of something I'd been drinking since October.

Then I read about it for a month, because I wanted to know whether I'd imagined it.

Cortisol is the stress hormone. It's supposed to move.

High in the morning to get you up. Sloping down across the day.

Lowest in the middle of the night.

That slope is what being a functioning person actually is.

Past 50, your body clears it more slowly. So instead of a slope you get a plateau.

It goes up in the morning and then it just stays up.

Flat at 2 in the afternoon, because there's no peak left to spend.

Awake at 3 in the morning, because there's no trough coming.

That was my whole complaint before any of this started. And it was one thing, not two.

And here is the part that actually explains night 8.

3 in the morning is the bottom of the curve. It is the hour your body is built to be least awake.

If you're already sitting flat at the top of your range all day, you have got nothing left to spend at 4am.

You don't fall asleep, necessarily. You just stop being able to see two numbers that don't match.

I'm not going to tell you a cup of coffee got me through my mother's death. Nothing gets you through that.

What it did was much smaller and much more specific. It kept me the kind of awake where I was still useful.

The thing I'd been drinking since October is Erth Superfood Brew.

It's real coffee, just low-acid.

600mg of KSM-66 ashwagandha, which is the standardized extract the human trials used. That's the one for cortisol.

500mg of lion's mane. Cordyceps, turkey tail, and real collagen.

Properly dosed and 3rd party tested, which is the reason I picked it over the others.

Plenty of bags say 2,000mg of 6 mushrooms and never tell you the split. It could be 1,900 of the cheapest one.

Plenty print the word ashwagandha, which on its own means almost nothing.

The ones naming KSM-66 were mostly nowhere near 600mg. I found 250mg in other brands more than once.

That's less than half the amount that actually makes a difference.

Here's the last thing.

I'd half-forgotten I was drinking it. That's the honest risk with something that works slowly - you stop noticing, and then you stop buying it.

I found out what it had been doing on the 8 nights it mattered.

Erth is 60% off right now with a free Starter Kit - frother and all - and a 45-day money-back guarantee.

Rated 4.9/5 across 16,000+ reviews.

I'd been on a mushroom coffee since the October before. My daughter put me on it.

The reason was boring. I'd stopped being able to do anything after 2 in the afternoon, and I'd been waking at 3 in the morning with my heart going for no reason I could name.

Went to the doctor twice. Blood's fine.

Told it was normal for my age and sent home.

So I'd decided I was just a woman who'd gone soft, and I stopped mentioning it.

By March I'd honestly half-forgotten I was drinking it.

The afternoons had quietly stopped being a problem and I'd stopped noticing there had ever been one.

Then my mother started dying, and I found out what it had been doing.

I'll tell you what a hospice night actually is.

It is not dramatic. That's the thing.

It's a chair, a lamp turned away from the bed, and a very long stretch of time.

You listen to breathing. That's the whole job.

You listen to breathing and you do not fall asleep.

You turn her every couple of hours. You do the mouth swabs.

You write down the time of everything on a sheet the nurse leaves.

And between those things there is nothing at all, for 40 minutes at a stretch, in a dark room, at 3 in the morning, when every part of your body is telling you to stop.

I drank a cup of that mushroom coffee at 9pm before every single one of those nights.

I'm aware that is not what it's for. I'm aware you're supposed to have it in the morning.

I didn't care. It was the only thing I had that worked.

Night 8.

The visiting nurse had been in that afternoon and there'd been a changeover - a different nurse from the one we'd had all week.

She left the handover sheet on the side like they do, with the times written on it.

At about 4 in the morning I was copying her last dose onto my sheet and something didn't sit right.

The interval on the handover sheet and the interval on the pharmacy label were not the same.

Now. I want to be careful here, because I'm not a nurse and this is not me being clever.

It was a 10-second thing. Two numbers next to each other that didn't match.

But you have to be awake to see two numbers not matching at 4 in the morning, and I was.

I called the after-hours line. They checked it.

The handover sheet was wrong.

They were very kind about it and told me it happens, and that I'd done the right thing calling.

I sat back down in that chair and shook for about 20 minutes.

She died on the 11th night, about 5:30 in the morning, and I was awake for it.

That matters to me more than I can explain to you.

She wasn't alone and she wasn't with somebody asleep in a chair. She was with her daughter, who was awake.

Afterwards I fell apart properly for about 3 weeks.

Flat, weepy, sleeping 11 hours and waking up tired, couldn't hold a thought.

Which I now understand is just what happens when you've been running on stress hormones for two weeks and then it stops.

But during it, I was a person I have never been.

So when it was over I sat down and worked out what was actually different about me.

And the only thing I could find was a cup of something I'd been drinking since October.

Then I read about it for a month, because I wanted to know whether I'd imagined it.

Cortisol is the stress hormone. It's supposed to move.

High in the morning to get you up. Sloping down across the day.

Lowest in the middle of the night.

That slope is what being a functioning person actually is.

Past 50, your body clears it more slowly. So instead of a slope you get a plateau.

It goes up in the morning and then it just stays up.

Flat at 2 in the afternoon, because there's no peak left to spend.

Awake at 3 in the morning, because there's no trough coming.

That was my whole complaint before any of this started. And it was one thing, not two.

And here is the part that actually explains night 8.

3 in the morning is the bottom of the curve. It is the hour your body is built to be least awake.

If you're already sitting flat at the top of your range all day, you have got nothing left to spend at 4am.

You don't fall asleep, necessarily. You just stop being able to see two numbers that don't match.

I'm not going to tell you a cup of coffee got me through my mother's death. Nothing gets you through that.

What it did was much smaller and much more specific. It kept me the kind of awake where I was still useful.

The ones naming KSM-66 were mostly nowhere near 600mg. I found 250mg in other brands more than once.
