Twelve weeks ago I wrote a short post asking a simple question.

I had just been diagnosed with dry age related macular degeneration.

My specialist had handed me a pamphlet for PreserVision and told me to come back in six months.

I had done about eight hours of my own reading that weekend and I had placed an order for a different supplement called Neurobella 15 in 1 Advanced Eye Formula.

I told anyone who happened to be reading that I would go back to the same specialist, on the same OCT machine, in exactly twelve weeks, and I would report back with the scan results.

No marketing. No sponsorship.

Just the numbers. I am back.

Here are the numbers. My name is Jennifer.

I am seventy two years old. I was a certified public accountant for forty three years.

You do not hire a CPA to embellish the report.

My diagnosis was October of last year.

The OCT scan showed eleven drusen deposits in the left macula and six in the right macula.

The largest drusen measured 167 microns in the left. The specialist classified it as intermediate dry AMD.

He said the word monitoring four times in a nine minute appointment. He said the word progression twice.

He did not once use the word reversal.

I drove home from the office in Hartford and sat in my driveway for about twenty minutes before I went inside because I did not want my wife Marjorie to see my face until I had it arranged.

I was a CPA for forty three years. I do not panic.

I document.

I went into my home office that night and opened a hardcover ruled ledger notebook I had used for personal records since the 1990s.

I started a new page. I wrote the date across the top.

I wrote the diagnosis under it. I wrote the specialist's name and the clinic address.

I wrote the drusen counts and the microns.

I made five column headings for a daily symptom log: DAY, READING LINE, NIGHT DRIVING, AMSLER GRID, NOTES.

And I started tracking.

Let me tell you what the first twelve weeks of that ledger looked like before I started on the Neurobella.

Because I want to be clear about what I was actually measuring.

Reading line.

I tracked the smallest line of print I could read with my glasses at a comfortable distance on a standard optometrist chart I had ordered online.

In October I was on line 7 of the chart. By Thanksgiving I was on line 6.

By Christmas I was on line 5. The line number was dropping about one line a month.

Night driving.

I tracked whether I was willing to drive after sunset on our road, which is a two lane county route.

In October I was still driving at night but I had stopped driving to my sister in law's house in New Britain because the interchange lights were bothering me.

By Thanksgiving I was not driving after sunset at all. Marjorie started taking the evening shopping runs.

Amsler grid.

I printed an Amsler grid and taped it to the wall of my office next to my desk.

Every morning I covered one eye and looked at the center dot.

In October I could see a slight wave in the top left quadrant of the grid when I looked with my left eye.

By Christmas the wave had a small gap in it where the lines visibly disappeared.

I photographed the grid with my phone once a week for my own records.

I placed the Neurobella order on January 6th. The bottle arrived January 9th.

I took the first capsule January 10th with my morning coffee. I updated the ledger that day.

I did not change anything else. No new glasses.

No new diet. No new exercise.

I did not stop the PreserVision because I had never been on it.

I started the Neurobella as a clean variable in a 12 week test on my own retinas, with my own ledger as the audit trail, and my own follow up OCT scan at the same clinic as the acceptance test.

Here is the part I did not write in the original post three months ago.

I am a 72 year old man who watched his own mother lose the top half of her central vision to AMD between 2003 and 2010.

I watched her stop recognizing her own grandchildren's faces at Sunday dinner.

I watched my father drive her to monthly eye appointments for seven years and come home quieter every time.

I watched her transition from reading her own mail, to asking me to read her mail, to asking me to explain why her own handwriting on a birthday card had become the equivalent of a blur.

I have known since the day my own diagnosis came in what the downstream cost of dry AMD is when you let the drusen grow.

I do not need the specialist to use the word reversal for me to know what a reversal would be worth.

Why did I pick Neurobella instead of PreserVision.

Because I did the thing my ledger habit makes me do with every major purchase, which is line up the candidates and compare the specifications.

I put the supplement facts panels of PreserVision, Ocuvite, and Neurobella side by side at my desk on a Saturday morning in January and I read them line by line under my desk lamp.

PreserVision and Ocuvite both contained Lutein and Zeaxanthin. Neither of them contained Meso Zeaxanthin.

Neurobella contained all three carotenoids in the ratios used in the Macular Pigment Optical Density studies I had pulled off PubMed that week.

Ten milligrams of Lutein. Two milligrams of Zeaxanthin.

Ten milligrams of Meso Zeaxanthin. I was not looking for a miracle.

I was looking for the bottle whose label matched the research. Only one of the three bottles did.

I want to be honest about something for the Most Aware reader.

You are probably reading this because you already know what Neurobella is.

You have probably already visited the product page at least once.

You have probably already read another native ad in this campaign.

You do not need me to re explain the mechanism to you.

You do not need the macular pigment optical density lecture. You have already done that reading.

What you need is receipts.

Here are the receipts.

Bottle one arrived January 9th. I finished bottle one on February 6th.

28 days, 28 capsules, zero missed doses.

Bottle two arrived February 4th. I finished bottle two on March 4th.

28 days, 28 capsules, zero missed doses.

Bottle three arrived March 2nd.

I am on day 27 of bottle three as of the morning I am writing this.

27 days, 27 capsules, zero missed doses.

Reading line week two of Neurobella I was still on line 5. Week four I was on line 5.

Week six I moved back to line 6. Week eight I moved back to line 7.

Week ten I held on line 7. Week twelve I am on line 8.

That is three lines of improvement on a standard optometrist chart across twelve weeks, which is the opposite direction of the trajectory I was on before I started the bottle.

Night driving week two I was still not driving at night.

Week four I drove to the end of our road after sunset and came back just to see.

Week six I drove to the grocery store.

Week eight I drove to my sister in law's in New Britain, including the interchange lights.

Week twelve I drove to Marjorie's sister's house in Springfield, Massachusetts, which is a 45 minute highway drive after dark that I had not done in over a year.

Amsler grid week two the wave and the gap in the top left of my left eye grid were still there.

Week four the gap was smaller but still visible. Week six I stopped seeing the gap at all.

Week eight and onward the top left quadrant of the grid looked straight and complete when I covered my right eye.

I still have a very faint wave in the far left edge of the left eye grid which I have photographed every Saturday since week eight so I can compare.

I will tell you what I was not expecting.

I was not expecting my follow up OCT scan to show smaller drusen.

I was hoping for smaller drusen but the honest prediction from my CPA brain was hold steady.

I went back to the specialist in Hartford on April 5th for the 12 week scan.

The technician took the scan. The specialist read the image.

He read it twice. He asked me what I was taking.

I told him. He wrote Neurobella on my chart in blue pen.

He said, Jennifer, your drusen are measurably smaller in both eyes.

The largest drusen in the left eye measured 142 microns on this scan, down from 167 on the October scan.

That is a 25 micron reduction in twelve weeks on a metric that is supposed to be getting larger.

He did not say a lot more.

He said, keep doing whatever you are doing, come back in six months.

I went out to the parking lot. I sat in the car.

I called Marjorie. I told her.

She cried.

I did not tell her I cried in the parking lot for about two minutes before I called her, but I did.

The scan printouts are sitting on my home office desk as I write this.

Week 0 on the left. Week 12 on the right.

A Neurobella bottle in between them.

I am going to photograph them and put the photograph in the comments of this post because I told the people who read the original post three months ago that I would bring receipts.

This is the receipts.

I do not know what is going to happen between week 12 and week 24.

I am going to keep taking the bottle every morning with my first cup of coffee and I am going to keep filling in the ledger and I am going to go back at week 24 for the next scan.

I will write another update. I will bring the next scan.

I will not embellish that one either.

Here are the two paths you have if you are reading this.

In path one you close the tab, you keep doing whatever you are doing, and you let the drusen do whatever drusen do on the six month monitoring schedule your specialist has you on.

In path two you click the link at the bottom of this post, you order the same bottle I ordered on January 6th, you take the first capsule tomorrow morning, and you start your own 12 week test on your own retinas with your own eyes as the measurement instrument.

The difference between the two paths is one click of a mouse and ninety days of consistency.

I cannot give my mother back the central vision she lost between 2003 and 2010.

I cannot give my father back the seven years he spent driving her to monthly appointments that never reversed the progression.

I grieve for those specific people because they are the reason I am writing this to strangers on the internet as a seventy two year old retired CPA.

But I can tell you what my own ledger says after twelve weeks.

I can tell you what my own scan says after twelve weeks.

I can tell you that the bottle I ordered on January 6th is the bottle I will still be ordering on January 6th of next year.

And I can tell you right now, while your own scan is still ahead of you and your own drusen still have room to move in the other direction.

Here is what I want you to understand.

Every morning between today and your next monitoring appointment is a morning your pigment layer is either rebuilding or thinning further.

There is no third option.

The supplement you take tomorrow morning either contains the three carotenoids the research supports or it does not.

The drusen in your macula are either getting smaller or they are getting larger.

This is not a situation that rewards delay.

It is a situation that rewards the decision to start a clean twelve week test on your own retinas as soon as possible.

I said at the beginning of this post that I was not going to embellish the report.

The link to the Neurobella product page is right below.

It is the same page I ordered from on January 6th.

The bottle is the same bottle I took for 84 consecutive mornings.

It comes with a ninety day money back guarantee which means if it does not move a single drusen in your own macula, you get every penny of the purchase price back.

You cannot get your drusen back if you wait. You can always get the money back.

The risk is entirely on the company, not on you. Click the link.

Order the first bottle. Start your own ledger on day one.

I will see you at week twelve.

Before you order lighted pine branches for your home, it's worth sitting with a few honest questions first.

I put this little buyer's guide together because product photos rarely tell you the things you actually need to know before you spend the money.

The photo running with this post is a side-by-side of the same room, taken from the same spot, at the same time of evening. The left side is labeled WITHOUT. The right side is labeled WITH. Nothing was rearranged between the two shots except one thing: the Enchanted Evergreen Pine from TwinklingTree, arranged in a plain vase and switched on.

The WITHOUT side isn't a bad room. It's clean, it's furnished, it's fine. It just reads a little flat once the sun goes down — the way most rooms do under overhead light. The WITH side is the same room with one soft point of warm golden light sitting on the table. That's the whole difference. And that's the honest scope of what this product does.

If you're deciding whether it belongs in your home, here is everything I'd want to know, laid out plainly.

1. How big is it, really?

Eighteen inches tall. That number matters more than any photo.

Eighteen inches means it's roughly the height of a table lamp without its shade. Tall enough to be noticed from across the room when it's lit. Small enough that it doesn't crowd a mantel, block a mirror, or take over a dining table.

If you were picturing a floor piece that fills a corner, this is not that. If you were picturing a little novelty trinket, it's not that either. It's an arrangement-sized piece — the scale you'd use for a vase of fresh branches from a florist.

A useful trick before you order: take a ruler or a rolled-up magazine, hold it at eighteen inches on the surface you're considering, and step back. If that height looks right in the spot, the scale will work.

2. What does it sit in?

Here's the part some listings gloss over, so I'll say it plainly: the vase is not included, and honestly, I think that's the right call.

These are loose Norfolk pine branches. You arrange them yourself in a vase you already own. I used a plain ceramic one from my own cabinet, and the arranging took maybe two minutes — set the branches in, spread them until they look natural, done.

Why does that matter? Because a vase packed in the box would match nobody's home. Your vase already matches your home. That's what keeps this from looking like a store display and starts making it look like something you put together yourself.

If you don't own a vase you like, a simple one from any home store will do. Heavier is better for stability. A wide mouth lets the branches fan out; a narrow one holds them more upright. Neither is wrong.

3. How bright is the glow — and will it keep you up at night?

This is decorative light, and I want to be direct about what that means.

The branches are threaded with small warm golden twinkles. Warm as in candlelight-colored, not the blue-white of a phone screen or an LED shop light. The glow is gentle enough to sit beside in the evening without it straining your eyes or dominating the room.

What it will not do is light your room. You will still turn on a lamp to read, still flip the switch when you cook. This is atmosphere, not illumination — the difference between a lit candle and a ceiling fixture. Any lighted branch sold as a lamp replacement is overpromising. This one doesn't need to.

A related worry, for anyone sensitive to light in the evening: warm gold at this scale is the gentlest category of decorative lighting there is. It's the tone of a low candle, not a screen. And since you switch it on and off yourself, the glow is there when you want it and gone when you don't.

What the WITH side of the photo shows is what actually happens: the nearby surfaces pick up a warm cast, the room gains a focal point after dark, and the space reads finished instead of flat. That's the honest job, and it does that job well.

4. Does it need an outlet?

No. It's battery powered, and that changes more than you'd expect.

Most of the best spots for a glow like this are exactly the spots with no outlet nearby — the middle of a mantel, the center of a dining table, an entryway console against a wall with nothing behind it. A corded piece forces you to decorate around the cord: hiding it behind books, taping it to the wall, or giving up on the spot altogether.

Cordless means you place it where it looks best, not where the wiring allows. It also means no white wire trailing down your mantel in the daytime, which is usually what gives away lighted decor before the lights even come on.

One practical note, because a buyer's guide should include it: batteries are batteries. You'll replace them from time to time, the same as a wall clock or a flameless candle. If you're the type who resents changing batteries in anything, weigh that honestly. For most people it's a fair trade for putting light in places lamps can't go.

5. Where does it actually work?

TwinklingTree suggests three placements on the official page, and they're the right three to consider.

The mantel. Eighteen inches is a comfortable mantel height — present without brushing the artwork or mirror above. If your mantel feels bare on one end, this fills it without a full styling project.

The table. On a dining table or side table, it works as a centerpiece you don't have to water, replace, or fuss over. On a smaller table beside a reading chair, it becomes the thing you switch on when you sit down for the evening.

The entryway. This might be the placement I'd argue for first. An entry console is the first surface you see coming home and the last one you pass at night. A soft golden glow there greets you at the door — and because it's cordless, an outlet-free entry table is no obstacle.

One piece, one spot, is the honest starting point. You don't need to buy three to find out whether you like it. Put it where you spend your evenings and see how the room feels after dark.

If you're torn between two spots, start where you sit longest after dinner. Decor earns its keep in the room where your evening actually happens — and at this size, it's easy to move if you change your mind.

6. Is it just a Christmas decoration?

Fair question, since pine is right there in the name.

Here's the distinction: Norfolk pine branches are a soft, graceful evergreen — closer to what a florist would put in a year-round arrangement than to a stiff Christmas-tree bough. There are no ornaments, no ribbon, no red-and-green anything. Greenery in a vase is a year-round look; it's the trimmings that make something read as December.

In November and December, it fits the season naturally. But in March, it's simply an evergreen arrangement with warm light in it — the way eucalyptus stems belong in any month. And the glow is golden, not multicolored, which matters more than people expect. Colored lights say holiday. Warm gold says evening.

If you'd feel obligated to box it up on January 2nd, you'd be boxing up a piece with nothing seasonal about it except the word pine. Mine stays out. It earns its place in July the same way it earns it in December: the room feels warmer after sunset with it than without it.

7. Will it look cheap up close?

This is the worry that stops most people, and it's a reasonable one, because plenty of lighted decor does look cheap — plastic-shiny needles, visible wire, lights so dense the greenery disappears.

A few things work in this piece's favor. Norfolk pine has naturally soft, feathery branching, an easier shape to render convincingly than stiff spruce. The twinkles are small and warm rather than large and glaring, so the light reads as glow, not bulbs. And because you arrange the branches yourself, they don't sit in the frozen, symmetrical pose that makes faux greenery look faux. Loose branches settled into your own vase carry the slight irregularity of a real arrangement — because it is one. You made it.

I'd also add: evening is when this piece does its work. Lit at dusk, in your vase, on your table, what registers is warm light through greenery. Nobody is inspecting needles by flashlight. And if you get it home and disagree, that's exactly what the guarantee below is for.

What it won't do

A fair guide includes the other column, so here it is.

It won't light your room. Covered above, but worth repeating: decorative glow, not functional lighting.

It won't fill a large empty corner. Eighteen inches is tabletop scale. If you need a six-foot statement piece, this isn't it.

It's indoor decor. It isn't made for a porch or patio.

It doesn't come with a vase. If you don't own one and don't want one, the branches will have nothing to stand in.

And it won't transform a room you dislike into a room you love. It does one thing: adds a warm, living-looking point of light to a surface after dark. As the photo shows, that one thing changes how a room feels in the evening. But it's an accent, and I'd rather you buy it as an accent than expect a renovation.

How much fussing does it take?

Some decor asks a lot of you. This asks for about two minutes, once.

You choose the vase. You set the branches in. You spread them until the shape pleases you — there is no wrong answer, since real arrangements aren't symmetrical either. Then you turn the lights on when you want them and off when you don't.

There's no watering, no wilting, no dropped needles to vacuum, no swapping stems when the season changes, no floral skills required. If you've ever put grocery-store flowers in water, you're overqualified.

That's worth naming, because plenty of us have quietly retired from decorating projects. Not from wanting a lovely home — from wanting one more thing to manage. This sits closer to a candle than a project: one small decision about placement, and then it simply does its evening job.

A quick way to decide

Here's the decision framework I'd offer a friend.

Skip it if: you want functional lighting, you need a large floor-standing piece, you want outdoor decor, or you'd resent ever changing a battery. None of those are what this is.

Consider it if: there's a surface in your home — a mantel end, an entry console, the table beside your chair — that looks fine by day and flat by night. That's the exact gap this fills. Look at your own room this evening after sunset and ask whether it resembles the WITHOUT photo. If it doesn't, you don't need this. If it does, you now know what the WITH version would look like, because the only variable between the two frames is this one piece, lit.

That's a more useful test than any adjective I could write.

The numbers, as of this writing

Price and terms change, so I'll date this: as of late August, the official TwinklingTree page shows the Enchanted Evergreen Pine at $39.99, marked down from $79.99 — a 50% reduction — with free shipping listed as a limited-time offer. Check the page for the current figures before you order; I'd rather you see today's terms than trust a Facebook post's memory.

One more thought about the price, since a guide should help you weigh it.

At $39.99 it sits in the range of a decent grocery-store bouquet and a half — except a bouquet is compost in ten days, and this is still on your mantel next year. If you're the sort who buys fresh flowers for the table, the math resolves quickly.

The guarantee, in plain terms

And there's something I need to tell you that I don't have time to explain in a 15-minute appointment.
Every week, I look into the eyes of diabetic patients who are watching the first signs appear. The microaneurysms. The tiny dot-like bleeds. The early changes that most doctors describe clinically, calmly, like they're reading a weather report.
I see what those words do to people in that chair.
I see the terror. I see the grief. I see the silent question they're too afraid to say out loud:
"Am I going to end up like my mother?"
And every week, I have to hand them a response that breaks my heart.
"We'll monitor it. Come back in six months. Try to keep your blood sugar controlled."
I watch their faces fall. I watch hope drain out of them in real time. I watch them leave my office believing the only road forward is the one they've already watched destroy someone they love — the needles, the laser sessions, the appointments that never end, the independence that disappears one visit at a time.
It is the worst part of my job.
Because here's what I cannot fully explain in a rushed appointment with three more patients waiting outside:
There IS a second road. Something most eye doctors never mention. Something that addresses where the damage actually starts — not in your bloodstream, but on a battlefield your entire current treatment was never built to reach.
And I'm going to tell you exactly what it is right now.
First, let me tell you what I see every single day in my practice.
I see 58-year-old women who have managed their Type 2 diabetes faithfully for over a decade — logging their meals, checking their blood sugar, taking every pill on schedule — sitting in my exam chair in shock because their last screening just showed "early changes."
I see patients who did everything right. Whose A1C numbers look fine. Who followed every instruction their endocrinologist gave them. And whose retinas are bleeding anyway.
I see the ones who watched their mothers go through this — Eylea injections every six weeks, laser sessions, $2,000 a needle, a medical system that shuffled them through "step therapy" like cattle and called it care — and who are sitting across from me with a single silent terror consuming them:
I am not doing that. I am not following her path. There has to be another way.
I see the guilt too. The quiet, devastating guilt that maybe they did this to themselves. That if they'd been more disciplined, caught it sooner, tried harder — they wouldn't be here.
I want to tell every single one of them: you didn't fail. But I don't have time. So I'm telling you now.
And I see the ones who come back too late. Who dismissed the early floaters — those little dark shapes that drift and dance in the corner of your eye, casting shadows over everything you try to look at, a constant reminder of how sick your eyes really are. Who ignored the blur that came and went — vision clear one hour and smeared the next, words on the page swimming, faces softening, never knowing if today was a good eye day or a bad one. Who stopped driving after dark because oncoming headlights exploded into blinding white starbursts, and slowly their world shrank to the hours before sunset — and told themselves that was just aging.
By the time I see those patients, I'm holding their hand in a room with very limited options.
I've watched patients describe waking up one morning to a dark red cloud slowly spreading across their vision — like a drop of ink dropped into a glass of water — terrified their sight is slipping away for good. That's vitreous hemorrhage. That's what advanced diabetic retinopathy looks like. And the people it happens to were standing exactly where you are standing now — at the early stage, with a window still open — when they decided to wait and see.
This is what keeps me up at night.
Because I know there's a window. I know that early intervention changes trajectories. I know that diabetic retinopathy does not have to end where your mother's ended.

But the system doesn't give me time to have that conversation.

So I'm having it now. With you. Right here.

Let me show you what I see when I examine a diabetic retina.

At the very back of your eye sits the retina — a thin layer of tissue packed with photoreceptors that translate light into everything you see. Running through it is a network of microscopic blood vessels, the smallest in the human body.

When blood sugar runs chronically elevated, it attacks those vessels. It stiffens their walls. It triggers oxidative damage that slowly corrodes their structural integrity. It drives inflammation that degrades the blood-retinal barrier — the wall that separates your bloodstream from the delicate tissue of the eye.

And then those walls begin to leak.

That is what your doctor saw in your screening. The tiny bleeds. The microaneurysms. The fluid weeping into retinal tissue it was never supposed to reach.

Now here is the part that no one explained to you. And this is the part that changes everything.

Your A1C measures sugar in your blood. But the damage I just described is not happening in your blood.

It is happening inside the eye itself — behind the blood-retinal barrier, in tissue your blood sugar management was never designed to reach. There are two battlefields. Your insulin, your pills, your diet, your finger-sticks — every single tool you have been handed fights on the first one: your bloodstream. The leaking, the swelling, the bleeding, the oxidative destruction happening right now between every appointment — that is all on the second battlefield. Deep inside the eye. Where nothing in your current treatment was ever built to go.

That is why you can do everything right. Log every meal. Bring your A1C to a perfect 5.7. And still sit in that exam chair and hear "there's new progression."

It feels like a punishment. Like your body is betraying you no matter what you do.

It isn't. You haven't been losing. You've been fighting in the wrong place. And nobody told you there was a second place to fight.

---

Here's what frustrates me about how this disease gets managed.

The medical system has one answer for diabetic retinopathy once it progresses far enough: injections. Anti-VEGF therapy. Eylea. Lucentis. Indefinitely. Every four to six weeks. Billed at two thousand dollars a needle, run through a step-therapy protocol designed more around insurance reimbursement than your quality of life.

I'm not saying those treatments don't have a place. In advanced disease, they do.

But they are deployed on the first battlefield. They reduce VEGF — the protein driving abnormal vessel growth — in the bloodstream and surrounding tissue. They do not rebuild the retinal capillary walls already damaged. They do not restore the oxidative defenses inside the eye that were stripped away years before the first injection was ever prescribed.

And they are presented to patients as the only road.

They are not.

---

Here's what the research shows — and what most eye doctors were never taught in medical school.

The retina has its own nutritional needs. Specific nutrients that physically cross the blood-retinal barrier, accumulate inside the retinal tissue, and go to work exactly where the damage is happening — on the second battlefield.

And the modern diabetic patient is almost universally depleted of them.

It starts with all three retinal carotenoids. Most doctors know about Lutein. Some know about Zeaxanthin. Almost none discuss Meso-Zeaxanthin — and its absence from most eye supplements is, in my opinion, one of the most significant nutritional blind spots in ophthalmology today.

Here's why all three matter:

Lutein concentrates in the peripheral macula. Zeaxanthin in the mid-peripheral region. Meso-Zeaxanthin at the very center — the fovea — where your sharpest, most critical vision is processed. Without all three, you are building a defense with holes in it. You're leaving the most important part of the macula unguarded.

→ 20mg of Lutein — most competitors use five to ten
→ 2mg of Zeaxanthin
→ 2mg of Meso-Zeaxanthin — which the diabetic eye can no longer synthesize efficiently on its own, and which nearly every supplement on the market skips entirely

Then comes the ingredient specifically studied for diabetic eyes — Alpha-Lipoic Acid. It is the only antioxidant that works in both the water-based and fat-based environments inside your cells, meaning it penetrates every compartment of retinal tissue. It also recharges the other antioxidants as they're spent, multiplying the effect of everything around it. Generic eye vitamins leave this out entirely. It should be the cornerstone of every diabetic eye formula. It is absent from almost all of them.

Then Astaxanthin — 6,000 times more powerful than Vitamin C at neutralizing the oxidative rust silently corroding your fragile capillary walls between every appointment. Those walls are what holds fluid where it belongs. When they weaken, they weep. The weeping is what your doctor is already seeing.

Ginkgo Biloba to drive blood flow back into the smallest retinal vessels that diabetes has been quietly starving of oxygen.

Taurine and Luteolin to support the retinal cells directly and calm the chronic low-grade inflammation burning through the blood-retinal barrier.

15 ingredients. One purpose. The second battlefield.

This does not touch your glucose. It does not interfere with your insulin, your metformin, or anything else your physician has prescribed. It does the one job your entire current treatment was never built to do — it shows up where the leaking actually begins.

---

Now let me speak directly to you.

If you're reading this and you've been told there are early changes in the back of your eye — microaneurysms, dot hemorrhages, the first signs — you are not at the end of this story.

You are at the beginning. And the beginning is the only moment where the gap between your mother's outcome and a different one is still wide open.

I have watched too many diabetic patients come to me too late. I have watched too many people lose the ability to read. Lose the ability to drive. Lose the ability to thread a needle or hold a newspaper at arm's length under a brighter and brighter lamp. Lose the ability to look across a room at their grandchild's smile and see it clearly.

I have watched people who were exactly where you are right now decide to wait and monitor — and come back two years later needing exactly the injections they were terrified of.

Don't be one of them.

When my own diabetic patients ask me what they can do beyond glycemic control, this formula is what I point them toward. Not because I say so. Because 24 years of watching this disease run its course on an undefended second battlefield tells me that doing nothing there is not a neutral choice.

It is a choice. It just doesn't feel like one until it's too late.

The time to act on the second battlefield is now. While the changes are early. While the gap is still open. While you still have something worth protecting.

Twelve weeks ago I wrote a short post asking a simple question.

I had just been diagnosed with dry age related macular degeneration.

My specialist had handed me a pamphlet for PreserVision and told me to come back in six months.

I had done about eight hours of my own reading that weekend and I had placed an order for a different supplement called Neurobella 15 in 1 Advanced Eye Formula.

I told anyone who happened to be reading that I would go back to the same specialist, on the same OCT machine, in exactly twelve weeks, and I would report back with the scan results.

No marketing. No sponsorship.

Just the numbers. I am back.

Here are the numbers. My name is Jennifer.

I am seventy two years old. I was a certified public accountant for forty three years.

You do not hire a CPA to embellish the report.

My diagnosis was October of last year.

The OCT scan showed eleven drusen deposits in the left macula and six in the right macula.

The largest drusen measured 167 microns in the left. The specialist classified it as intermediate dry AMD.

He said the word monitoring four times in a nine minute appointment. He said the word progression twice.

He did not once use the word reversal.

I drove home from the office in Hartford and sat in my driveway for about twenty minutes before I went inside because I did not want my wife Marjorie to see my face until I had it arranged.

I was a CPA for forty three years. I do not panic.

I document.

I went into my home office that night and opened a hardcover ruled ledger notebook I had used for personal records since the 1990s.

I started a new page. I wrote the date across the top.

I wrote the diagnosis under it. I wrote the specialist's name and the clinic address.

I wrote the drusen counts and the microns.

I made five column headings for a daily symptom log: DAY, READING LINE, NIGHT DRIVING, AMSLER GRID, NOTES.

And I started tracking.

Let me tell you what the first twelve weeks of that ledger looked like before I started on the Neurobella.

Because I want to be clear about what I was actually measuring.

Reading line.

I tracked the smallest line of print I could read with my glasses at a comfortable distance on a standard optometrist chart I had ordered online.

In October I was on line 7 of the chart. By Thanksgiving I was on line 6.

By Christmas I was on line 5. The line number was dropping about one line a month.

Night driving.

I tracked whether I was willing to drive after sunset on our road, which is a two lane county route.

In October I was still driving at night but I had stopped driving to my sister in law's house in New Britain because the interchange lights were bothering me.

By Thanksgiving I was not driving after sunset at all. Marjorie started taking the evening shopping runs.

Amsler grid.

I printed an Amsler grid and taped it to the wall of my office next to my desk.

Every morning I covered one eye and looked at the center dot.

In October I could see a slight wave in the top left quadrant of the grid when I looked with my left eye.

By Christmas the wave had a small gap in it where the lines visibly disappeared.

I photographed the grid with my phone once a week for my own records.

I placed the Neurobella order on January 6th. The bottle arrived January 9th.

I took the first capsule January 10th with my morning coffee. I updated the ledger that day.

I did not change anything else. No new glasses.

No new diet. No new exercise.

I did not stop the PreserVision because I had never been on it.

I started the Neurobella as a clean variable in a 12 week test on my own retinas, with my own ledger as the audit trail, and my own follow up OCT scan at the same clinic as the acceptance test.

Here is the part I did not write in the original post three months ago.

I am a 72 year old man who watched his own mother lose the top half of her central vision to AMD between 2003 and 2010.

I watched her stop recognizing her own grandchildren's faces at Sunday dinner.

I watched my father drive her to monthly eye appointments for seven years and come home quieter every time.

I watched her transition from reading her own mail, to asking me to read her mail, to asking me to explain why her own handwriting on a birthday card had become the equivalent of a blur.

I do not need the specialist to use the word reversal for me to know what a reversal would be worth.

Because I did the thing my ledger habit makes me do with every major purchase, which is line up the candidates and compare the specifications.

You have probably already read another native ad in this campaign.

Every night since August 21st, at about 10:40, my phone has buzzed with a photo from my daughter.

For the first 16 nights, it was a needle.

This is the story of what's in those photos.

Picture a dorm room desk 6 hours north of Boise. A lamp from our basement that used to be in the guest room. A laptop, a water bottle covered in stickers, and a half eaten sleeve of crackers.

Picture my daughter at that desk at 10:40 at night, in the gray hoodie she took from her dad's closet in June and never gave back.

And picture me, 6 hours south, on the couch with my phone in my lap, pretending to watch TV and waiting.

That's how this whole thing started. Nobody planned it, nobody said a word. And it's kept going the same way.

To explain the photos I have to explain us.

I'm Lisa. I'm 51. I've worked at the same credit union in Boise for 22 years. I can tell you what's in your checking account without looking, but I can't sew on a button.

My husband Mark sells farm equipment, which means he's either on the road or out in the yard.

Hannah is our only kid. She turned 18 in May.

For 18 years my life was shaped exactly like hers.

Bus at 7:10. Practice till 5:30. Dinner whenever everyone got home.

4 years of high school theater, which means 4 years of me making costumes with a hot glue gun at midnight, because, again, I can't sew.

I'm not complaining. I loved it. I loved every single loud second of it.

And then on August 20th we drove her 6 hours north, carried 11 boxes up 3 flights of stairs, made her bed, met her roommate's parents, and drove home.

Mark drove. Neither of us turned the radio on, which if you know Mark, is a first.

We stopped for gas in a little town halfway and I bought a pack of Juicy Fruit, out of habit. I've been buying her Juicy Fruit since she had baby teeth. I put it in the cup holder.

Its still there.

People tell you the quiet is the worst part and I didn't beleive them. The house got quiet in a way I wasn't ready for. Her door stayed open. Mark started eating dinner standing at the counter like a bachelor. Our dog went and sat by the front door at 3:15 every afternoon for a week, because that's when the school bus used to come.

Here is the part I didn't tell anyone, not even Mark.

When I was in college my mother called me every Sunday at 6 o'clock. I was in a dorm in Pocatello and the phone was at the end of the hall. I'd talk to her for 10 minutes, standing up, with people walking past behind me.

I did that for 4 years.

I don't remember one single thing we said.

She passed 4 years ago. I would give almost anything to remember one of those Sundays.

So I knew, going in, what I didn't want. I didn't want a Sunday phone call that neither of us would remember.

I wanted something smaller. Something every day. I wanted Hannah to think of me for a minute, without it being a chore.

My grandmother made the quilt on our bed. She's been gone 20 years and I still can't fold it without thinking about her hands. Things people make for you do that. They hold on to a little piece of the person.

I didn't need Hannah to think about me all day. I just wanted to be in her hands for a minute.

Which is how a woman who glues costumes ended up buying a kit to make a handbag.

Hannah had said all summer she wanted a crossbody for campus, something to keep her ID and her keys in so she'd stop losing them. She has lost 4 sets of keys. I counted.

And I thought, if she makes it herself, then every time she picks up that needle she'll think, my mom gave me this.

That was the whole plan. It wasn't a very good plan. I didn't even know if she'd open it.

On move in day, while she was down the hall meeting people, I put the kit in the plastic bin under her bed. Between the extra towels and a 12 pack of ramen.

No note. I didn't say a word about it.

I figured she'd find it when she went looking for a towel.

She found it the next night.

At 10:41 my phone buzzed. A photo. A needle pushed halfway through the first hole of 2 pieces, her thumb holding them together.

Under it, one line. "is this right???"

I had no idea. I wrote back "ask the video."

The next night at 10:38, another photo. 2 more pieces.

No words this time. Just the photo.

I sent back a heart.

And that was it. That was the deal. We never talked about it. We never agreed on anything. A photo comes, a heart goes back.

It's happened every night since.

Mark pretends he isn't part of it. But around 10:35 he comes in from the garage, sits on the arm of the couch and says "Anything yet?" like he's asking about the weather.

Now here's what I'd been doing before the photos started, in those first 2 days. Maybe you've done it too.

I texted "How was your day?" I got back "good."

I called at 6, like my mother did. Hannah picked up and said "Mom I'm with people," and I heard laughing behind her, which is exactly what I wanted for her, and it still sent me to the laundry room to cry for a minute.

I mailed a box of cookies. They got there as crumbs.

The family group chat got a thumbs up.

None of that was wrong. None of it was too much. It just didn't fit.

That took me a while to understand.

A phone call at 6 is shaped like my day, not hers. Her day doesn't have a 6 o'clock in it anymore. It has a 10:40.

"How was your day" asks her to come up with something. A photo just asks her to point her phone at what's already in front of her.

And what was in front of her, it turned out, was her whole new life.

Night 3, 2 pieces side by side on the desk under the basement lamp.

Night 5, the video paused on her laptop, with her finger pointing at the screen like she was telling on it.

Night 7, a hand that wasn't hers holding the strap. Under it, "roommate says hi." That was the first time I ever saw Priya. A hand.

Night 9, one stitch, very crooked. "redoing this 😤"

Night 12, the pieces on her bed next to a stack of index cards for her first chemistry test.

Night 14, the window by her desk with rain on it, and the handbag blurry in the corner, almost by accident.

Night 16, the last piece, and a thumbs up.

Somewhere around night 10 I realized what was happening.

She wasn't sending me a handbag.

She was sending me her room. Her desk. Her roommate. Her weather. The one quiet minute of her day, the one minute small enough to share.

The handbag was just the reason to point the phone.

I'd bought it so she would think of me. It turned out to work the other way too. Every night at 10:40 I was thinking about her, and for the first time since August it didn't hurt.

It's never really about the thing, is it. A plate of food on a neighbor's step, a card in the mail, a kit in a bin. It's a shape for 2 people to talk in, when the regular shapes don't fit anymore.

I want to tell you plainly what was in the box, because when I bought it I didn't really know either.

The kit is from a company called Craftiva. Every piece is already cut. The holes are already punched. All the hardware is in the box, and there are written steps and a video for every step. No sewing machine. No experience. The website says most people finish in 1 to 4 hours.

Hannah made hers last 16 nights, a few steps at a time. I'm glad she did. I'd of been heartbroken at 4 hours.

The one she made is the Liliora in black.

One kit is $49. They had 2 kits for $79, so I bought 2 and told myself the second one was a spare, in case she lost a piece. Remember that spare.

There's a 30 day money back guarantee too. I read it twice, because credit union.

And now the honest part, because I don't want you to read this and think a kit did something it didn't.

A handbag kit does not keep your kid close. Hannah did that. The kit is pieces and thread and a video. The rest was all her.

Some nights the photo came at 1 in the morning. Some nights it was a blurry picture of her ceiling. I had to learn not to read anything into it.

It isn't a phone call, and it isn't a hug at the airport. If your kid calls you on Sundays, keep picking up.

But if your kid is about to leave, and you're scared of the quiet like I was, this gave the quiet a shape. It gave both of us something to do at 10:40 besides miss each other.

The ending is small, and there are 2 of them.

The first one was family weekend, the first weekend of October.

Mark and I drove the 6 hours north. Hannah came across the lawn in front of her dorm to meet us with the handbag across her body. Black, with her student ID and her keys inside it, which is a first in recorded history.

She didn't say anything about it. She didn't have to.

I'd watched it get made, one photo at a time, from 6 hours away.

We had dinner at a pizza place she picked. She showed me where night 9 was. You can't even tell. Then she set the handbag on the seat next to her like it was a person, and when Mark reached for it she said "Careful," and he put his hands up like he'd been caught.

The second ending is still going.

The handbag was finished on September 5th.

The photos didn't stop.

They aren't needles anymore. They're a burrito the size of her head. Her first chemistry test, a B+, held up next to her face. The sunset from the 3rd floor. A squirrel she swears stole a whole bagel.

Still around 10:40. Still no conversation. A photo comes, a heart goes back.

And 2 weeks ago I finally opened the spare. It was never a spare. It was mine the whole time.

So now, some nights at 10:40, the needle photo goes the other way.

My stitches are worse than hers. She tells me so, with alot of crying laughing faces.

Last week Mark asked if they make a kit for men. I said it's a handbag kit, Mark. He said he's thinking about it.

One of us has a life shaped like a dorm room. One of us has a life shaped like an empty bedroom down the hall.

It turns out you can pass something between them.

It just has to be small enough to fit in a photo.

P.S. If you're about to drop a kid off somewhere, here's my one piece of advice. Don't announce it. Put it in the bin under the bed and let them find it. The whole point is that it's theirs.

P.P.S. What it is, plainly. A handbag kit. Every piece cut, holes punched, hardware in the box, written steps and videos. $49 for one, or 2 for $79 right now, with a 30 day money back guarantee.

P.P.P.S. If you're the kid reading this, send your mom a photo tonight. Of anything at all. She'll know what it means.

I'm a retina specialist. I've been treating diabetic eye disease for 24 years.
And there's something I need to tell you that I don't have time to explain in a 15-minute appointment.
Every week, I look into the eyes of diabetic patients who are watching the first signs appear. The microaneurysms. The tiny dot-like bleeds. The early changes that most doctors describe clinically, calmly, like they're reading a weather report.
I see what those words do to people in that chair.
I see the terror. I see the grief. I see the silent question they're too afraid to say out loud:
"Am I going to end up like my mother?"
And every week, I have to hand them a response that breaks my heart.
"We'll monitor it. Come back in six months. Try to keep your blood sugar controlled."
I watch their faces fall. I watch hope drain out of them in real time. I watch them leave my office believing the only road forward is the one they've already watched destroy someone they love — the needles, the laser sessions, the appointments that never end, the independence that disappears one visit at a time.
It is the worst part of my job.
Because here's what I cannot fully explain in a rushed appointment with three more patients waiting outside:
There IS a second road. Something most eye doctors never mention. Something that addresses where the damage actually starts — not in your bloodstream, but on a battlefield your entire current treatment was never built to reach.
And I'm going to tell you exactly what it is right now.
First, let me tell you what I see every single day in my practice.
I see 58-year-old women who have managed their Type 2 diabetes faithfully for over a decade — logging their meals, checking their blood sugar, taking every pill on schedule — sitting in my exam chair in shock because their last screening just showed "early changes."
I see patients who did everything right. Whose A1C numbers look fine. Who followed every instruction their endocrinologist gave them. And whose retinas are bleeding anyway.
I see the ones who watched their mothers go through this — Eylea injections every six weeks, laser sessions, $2,000 a needle, a medical system that shuffled them through "step therapy" like cattle and called it care — and who are sitting across from me with a single silent terror consuming them:
I am not doing that. I am not following her path. There has to be another way.
I see the guilt too. The quiet, devastating guilt that maybe they did this to themselves. That if they'd been more disciplined, caught it sooner, tried harder — they wouldn't be here.
I want to tell every single one of them: you didn't fail. But I don't have time. So I'm telling you now.
And I see the ones who come back too late. Who dismissed the early floaters — those little dark shapes that drift and dance in the corner of your eye, casting shadows over everything you try to look at, a constant reminder of how sick your eyes really are. Who ignored the blur that came and went — vision clear one hour and smeared the next, words on the page swimming, faces softening, never knowing if today was a good eye day or a bad one. Who stopped driving after dark because oncoming headlights exploded into blinding white starbursts, and slowly their world shrank to the hours before sunset — and told themselves that was just aging.
By the time I see those patients, I'm holding their hand in a room with very limited options.
I've watched patients describe waking up one morning to a dark red cloud slowly spreading across their vision — like a drop of ink dropped into a glass of water — terrified their sight is slipping away for good. That's vitreous hemorrhage. That's what advanced diabetic retinopathy looks like. And the people it happens to were standing exactly where you are standing now — at the early stage, with a window still open — when they decided to wait and see.
This is what keeps me up at night.
Because I know there's a window. I know that early intervention changes trajectories. I know that diabetic retinopathy does not have to end where your mother's ended.

But the system doesn't give me time to have that conversation.

So I'm having it now. With you. Right here.

---

If you have Type 2 diabetes and you've been told there are early changes in the back of your eye — please pay close attention to what I'm about to explain.

These are not just complications of blood sugar. Something very specific is happening inside your eye. And understanding it is the difference between the road your mother walked and a different one entirely.

Let me show you what I see when I examine a diabetic retina.

At the very back of your eye sits the retina — a thin layer of tissue packed with photoreceptors that translate light into everything you see. Running through it is a network of microscopic blood vessels, the smallest in the human body.

When blood sugar runs chronically elevated, it attacks those vessels. It stiffens their walls. It triggers oxidative damage that slowly corrodes their structural integrity. It drives inflammation that degrades the blood-retinal barrier — the wall that separates your bloodstream from the delicate tissue of the eye.

And then those walls begin to leak.

That is what your doctor saw in your screening. The tiny bleeds. The microaneurysms. The fluid weeping into retinal tissue it was never supposed to reach.

Now here is the part that no one explained to you. And this is the part that changes everything.

Your A1C measures sugar in your blood. But the damage I just described is not happening in your blood.

It is happening inside the eye itself — behind the blood-retinal barrier, in tissue your blood sugar management was never designed to reach. There are two battlefields. Your insulin, your pills, your diet, your finger-sticks — every single tool you have been handed fights on the first one: your bloodstream. The leaking, the swelling, the bleeding, the oxidative destruction happening right now between every appointment — that is all on the second battlefield. Deep inside the eye. Where nothing in your current treatment was ever built to go.

That is why you can do everything right. Log every meal. Bring your A1C to a perfect 5.7. And still sit in that exam chair and hear "there's new progression."

It feels like a punishment. Like your body is betraying you no matter what you do.

It isn't. You haven't been losing. You've been fighting in the wrong place. And nobody told you there was a second place to fight.

---

Here's what frustrates me about how this disease gets managed.

The medical system has one answer for diabetic retinopathy once it progresses far enough: injections. Anti-VEGF therapy. Eylea. Lucentis. Indefinitely. Every four to six weeks. Billed at two thousand dollars a needle, run through a step-therapy protocol designed more around insurance reimbursement than your quality of life.

I'm not saying those treatments don't have a place. In advanced disease, they do.

But they are deployed on the first battlefield. They reduce VEGF — the protein driving abnormal vessel growth — in the bloodstream and surrounding tissue. They do not rebuild the retinal capillary walls already damaged. They do not restore the oxidative defenses inside the eye that were stripped away years before the first injection was ever prescribed.

And they are presented to patients as the only road.

They are not.

---

Here's what the research shows — and what most eye doctors were never taught in medical school.

The retina has its own nutritional needs. Specific nutrients that physically cross the blood-retinal barrier, accumulate inside the retinal tissue, and go to work exactly where the damage is happening — on the second battlefield.

And the modern diabetic patient is almost universally depleted of them.

It starts with all three retinal carotenoids. Most doctors know about Lutein. Some know about Zeaxanthin. Almost none discuss Meso-Zeaxanthin — and its absence from most eye supplements is, in my opinion, one of the most significant nutritional blind spots in ophthalmology today.

Here's why all three matter:

Lutein concentrates in the peripheral macula. Zeaxanthin in the mid-peripheral region. Meso-Zeaxanthin at the very center — the fovea — where your sharpest, most critical vision is processed. Without all three, you are building a defense with holes in it. You're leaving the most important part of the macula unguarded.

The formula I'm about to describe contains:
→ 20mg of Lutein — most competitors use five to ten
→ 2mg of Zeaxanthin
→ 2mg of Meso-Zeaxanthin — which the diabetic eye can no longer synthesize efficiently on its own, and which nearly every supplement on the market skips entirely

Then comes the ingredient specifically studied for diabetic eyes — Alpha-Lipoic Acid. It is the only antioxidant that works in both the water-based and fat-based environments inside your cells, meaning it penetrates every compartment of retinal tissue. It also recharges the other antioxidants as they're spent, multiplying the effect of everything around it. Generic eye vitamins leave this out entirely. It should be the cornerstone of every diabetic eye formula. It is absent from almost all of them.

Then Astaxanthin — 6,000 times more powerful than Vitamin C at neutralizing the oxidative rust silently corroding your fragile capillary walls between every appointment. Those walls are what holds fluid where it belongs. When they weaken, they weep. The weeping is what your doctor is already seeing.

Bilberry Extract at 50mg, standardized for anthocyanins — used in European ophthalmology for decades to structurally reinforce tiny vessel walls so they hold instead of hemorrhage.

Ginkgo Biloba to drive blood flow back into the smallest retinal vessels that diabetes has been quietly starving of oxygen.

And the complete AREDS2 foundation — Vitamin C, Vitamin E as mixed tocopherols, Omega-3 fatty acids, and Zinc and Copper in the precise ratio that prevents one from depleting the other.

15 ingredients. One purpose. The second battlefield.

This does not touch your glucose. It does not interfere with your insulin, your metformin, or anything else your physician has prescribed. It does the one job your entire current treatment was never built to do — it shows up where the leaking actually begins.

---

Now let me speak directly to you.

If you're reading this and you've been told there are early changes in the back of your eye — microaneurysms, dot hemorrhages, the first signs — you are not at the end of this story.

You are at the beginning. And the beginning is the only moment where the gap between your mother's outcome and a different one is still wide open.

I have watched too many diabetic patients come to me too late. I have watched too many people lose the ability to read. Lose the ability to drive. Lose the ability to thread a needle or hold a newspaper at arm's length under a brighter and brighter lamp. Lose the ability to look across a room at their grandchild's smile and see it clearly.

I have watched people who were exactly where you are right now decide to wait and monitor — and come back two years later needing exactly the injections they were terrified of.

Don't be one of them.

When my own diabetic patients ask me what they can do beyond glycemic control, this formula is what I point them toward. Not because I say so. Because 24 years of watching this disease run its course on an undefended second battlefield tells me that doing nothing there is not a neutral choice.

It is a choice. It just doesn't feel like one until it's too late.

It carries a 90-day money-back guarantee. If you don't notice meaningful improvement in your visual comfort and clarity, you receive a full refund — even if you've used the entire supply.

You said you are not following your mother's path. You said you are not going on injections for the rest of your life. You said there has to be another way.

There is. But the window to use it is not unlimited. Every month without targeted nutritional defense inside the eye is another month of uncontested oxidative damage to your retinal tissue — happening silently, between appointments, on a battlefield your blood sugar control has never reached.

The time to act on the second battlefield is now. While the changes are early. While the gap is still open. While you still have something worth protecting.

Twelve weeks ago I wrote a short post asking a simple question.

I had just been diagnosed with dry age related macular degeneration.

My specialist had handed me a pamphlet for PreserVision and told me to come back in six months.

I had done about eight hours of my own reading that weekend and I had placed an order for a different supplement called Neurobella 15 in 1 Advanced Eye Formula.

I told anyone who happened to be reading that I would go back to the same specialist, on the same OCT machine, in exactly twelve weeks, and I would report back with the scan results.

No marketing. No sponsorship.

Just the numbers. I am back.

Here are the numbers. My name is Jennifer.

I am seventy two years old. I was a certified public accountant for forty three years.

You do not hire a CPA to embellish the report.

My diagnosis was October of last year.

The OCT scan showed eleven drusen deposits in the left macula and six in the right macula.

The largest drusen measured 167 microns in the left. The specialist classified it as intermediate dry AMD.

He said the word monitoring four times in a nine minute appointment. He said the word progression twice.

He did not once use the word reversal.

I drove home from the office in Hartford and sat in my driveway for about twenty minutes before I went inside because I did not want my wife Marjorie to see my face until I had it arranged.

I was a CPA for forty three years. I do not panic.

I document.

I went into my home office that night and opened a hardcover ruled ledger notebook I had used for personal records since the 1990s.

I started a new page. I wrote the date across the top.

I wrote the diagnosis under it. I wrote the specialist's name and the clinic address.

I wrote the drusen counts and the microns.

I made five column headings for a daily symptom log: DAY, READING LINE, NIGHT DRIVING, AMSLER GRID, NOTES.

And I started tracking.

Let me tell you what the first twelve weeks of that ledger looked like before I started on the Neurobella.

Because I want to be clear about what I was actually measuring.

Reading line.

I tracked the smallest line of print I could read with my glasses at a comfortable distance on a standard optometrist chart I had ordered online.

In October I was on line 7 of the chart. By Thanksgiving I was on line 6.

By Christmas I was on line 5. The line number was dropping about one line a month.

Night driving.

I tracked whether I was willing to drive after sunset on our road, which is a two lane county route.

In October I was still driving at night but I had stopped driving to my sister in law's house in New Britain because the interchange lights were bothering me.

By Thanksgiving I was not driving after sunset at all. Marjorie started taking the evening shopping runs.

Amsler grid.

I printed an Amsler grid and taped it to the wall of my office next to my desk.

Every morning I covered one eye and looked at the center dot.

In October I could see a slight wave in the top left quadrant of the grid when I looked with my left eye.

By Christmas the wave had a small gap in it where the lines visibly disappeared.

I photographed the grid with my phone once a week for my own records.

I placed the Neurobella order on January 6th. The bottle arrived January 9th.

I took the first capsule January 10th with my morning coffee. I updated the ledger that day.

I did not change anything else. No new glasses.

No new diet. No new exercise.

I did not stop the PreserVision because I had never been on it.

I started the Neurobella as a clean variable in a 12 week test on my own retinas, with my own ledger as the audit trail, and my own follow up OCT scan at the same clinic as the acceptance test.

Here is the part I did not write in the original post three months ago.

I am a 72 year old man who watched his own mother lose the top half of her central vision to AMD between 2003 and 2010.

I watched her stop recognizing her own grandchildren's faces at Sunday dinner.

I watched my father drive her to monthly eye appointments for seven years and come home quieter every time.

I watched her transition from reading her own mail, to asking me to read her mail, to asking me to explain why her own handwriting on a birthday card had become the equivalent of a blur.

I have known since the day my own diagnosis came in what the downstream cost of dry AMD is when you let the drusen grow.

I do not need the specialist to use the word reversal for me to know what a reversal would be worth.

Why did I pick Neurobella instead of PreserVision.

Because I did the thing my ledger habit makes me do with every major purchase, which is line up the candidates and compare the specifications.

I put the supplement facts panels of PreserVision, Ocuvite, and Neurobella side by side at my desk on a Saturday morning in January and I read them line by line under my desk lamp.

PreserVision and Ocuvite both contained Lutein and Zeaxanthin. Neither of them contained Meso Zeaxanthin.

Neurobella contained all three carotenoids in the ratios used in the Macular Pigment Optical Density studies I had pulled off PubMed that week.

Ten milligrams of Lutein. Two milligrams of Zeaxanthin.

Ten milligrams of Meso Zeaxanthin. I was not looking for a miracle.

I was looking for the bottle whose label matched the research. Only one of the three bottles did.

I want to be honest about something for the Most Aware reader.

You are probably reading this because you already know what Neurobella is.

You have probably already visited the product page at least once.

You have probably already read another native ad in this campaign.

You do not need me to re explain the mechanism to you.

You do not need the macular pigment optical density lecture. You have already done that reading.

What you need is receipts.

Here are the receipts.

Bottle one arrived January 9th. I finished bottle one on February 6th.

28 days, 28 capsules, zero missed doses.

Bottle two arrived February 4th. I finished bottle two on March 4th.

28 days, 28 capsules, zero missed doses.

Bottle three arrived March 2nd.

I am on day 27 of bottle three as of the morning I am writing this.

27 days, 27 capsules, zero missed doses.

Reading line week two of Neurobella I was still on line 5. Week four I was on line 5.

Week six I moved back to line 6. Week eight I moved back to line 7.

Week ten I held on line 7. Week twelve I am on line 8.

That is three lines of improvement on a standard optometrist chart across twelve weeks, which is the opposite direction of the trajectory I was on before I started the bottle.

Night driving week two I was still not driving at night.

Week four I drove to the end of our road after sunset and came back just to see.

Week six I drove to the grocery store.

Week eight I drove to my sister in law's in New Britain, including the interchange lights.

Week twelve I drove to Marjorie's sister's house in Springfield, Massachusetts, which is a 45 minute highway drive after dark that I had not done in over a year.

Amsler grid week two the wave and the gap in the top left of my left eye grid were still there.

Week four the gap was smaller but still visible. Week six I stopped seeing the gap at all.

Week eight and onward the top left quadrant of the grid looked straight and complete when I covered my right eye.

I still have a very faint wave in the far left edge of the left eye grid which I have photographed every Saturday since week eight so I can compare.

I will tell you what I was not expecting.

I was not expecting my follow up OCT scan to show smaller drusen.

I was hoping for smaller drusen but the honest prediction from my CPA brain was hold steady.

I went back to the specialist in Hartford on April 5th for the 12 week scan.

The technician took the scan. The specialist read the image.

He read it twice. He asked me what I was taking.

I told him. He wrote Neurobella on my chart in blue pen.

He said, Jennifer, your drusen are measurably smaller in both eyes.

The largest drusen in the left eye measured 142 microns on this scan, down from 167 on the October scan.

That is a 25 micron reduction in twelve weeks on a metric that is supposed to be getting larger.

He did not say a lot more.

He said, keep doing whatever you are doing, come back in six months.

I went out to the parking lot. I sat in the car.

I called Marjorie. I told her.

She cried.

I did not tell her I cried in the parking lot for about two minutes before I called her, but I did.

I see what those words do to people in that chair.
I see the terror. I see the grief. I see the silent question they're too afraid to say out loud:
"Am I going to end up like my mother?"
And every week, I have to hand them a response that breaks my heart.
"We'll monitor it. Come back in six months. Try to keep your blood sugar controlled."
I watch their faces fall. I watch hope drain out of them in real time. I watch them leave my office believing the only road forward is the one they've already watched destroy someone they love — the needles, the laser sessions, the appointments that never end, the independence that disappears one visit at a time.

At the very back of your eye sits the retina — a thin layer of tissue packed with photoreceptors that translate light into everything you see. Running through it is a network of microscopic blood vessels, the smallest in the human body.

When blood sugar runs chronically elevated, it attacks those vessels. It stiffens their walls. It triggers oxidative damage that slowly corrodes their structural integrity. If you're reading this and you've been told there are early changes in the back of your eye — microaneurysms, dot hemorrhages, the first signs — you are not at the end of this story.
